articles.title: The politics of stasis and change: The motivational roots of conservatism in party platforms and citizens' own words
articles.authors: Yael Ecker; Joris Lammers
articles.abstract: A central question in political psychology concerns the motivational roots of ideological differences between left and right. A common approach explains right-wing thinking as reflecting heightened sensitivity to threat and a motivation to protect the status quo. We argue that this approach rests on an incomplete model of goals, which overlooks the motive to conserve. Building on the ternary goal model, we examine whether the right is better characterized by maintenance (sustaining a valued present) than by protection (responding to threats). Using a multilingual classifier validated on human-rated statements, we measured goals in a top-down manner, in 892 party platforms from 11 countries, and bottom-up, in the goals spontaneously reported by 2,333 citizens in six countries and in citizens’ support for platform statements that differed in goal orientation. Top-down, right-wing parties were more maintenance-oriented than left-wing parties, and in recent decades less progress-oriented. Protection orientation did not differ by side but was higher in opposition and at the ideological margins. Bottom-up, citizens showed a similar pattern. Progress orientation was strongest on the left. Maintenance orientation followed a curve that peaked among moderate conservatives. Its linear rise with conservatism was suppressed by institutional trust, which was lower on the right. In support ratings, progress-oriented statements appealed more to the left and maintenance-oriented statements more to the right, whereas protection-oriented statements favored neither. The left–right divide thus sets two constructive aims – to progress and to maintain – against each other, while protection marks those in opposition and at the margins.

articles.title: From Phonological Skills to Reading Fluency: The Mediating Role of Reading Prosody
articles.authors: Petra Kóródi; Ferenc Honbolygó
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The development of reading fluency relies on phonological skills and prosodic competence, but evidence about the developmental mechanisms underlying this relationship remain scarce. Previous research has relied on subjective rating scales or adult-based acoustic comparisons, mostly in stress-timed languages. This study investigated whether objective acoustic markers of oral reading prosody mediate the relationship between cognitive skills (phonological awareness [PA] and rapid automatized naming [RAN]) and reading fluency in a syllable-timed language.
Method: The sample consisted of 56 typically developing, Hungarian-speaking primary school children (Mage = 8.96 years, 55,36% boys) who completed standardized cognitive assessments. Prosodic competence was measured by comparing acoustic features from an oral reading task against each child's own prosodic imitation baseline, using dynamic time warping to align melodic and rhythmic contours. Data were analyzed using path analysis.
Results: Temporal features, especially tempo stability, emerged as the strongest predictor of reading fluency, whereas melodic and rhythmic markers added no unique variance. Path analysis revealed that RAN predicted reading fluency directly, while PA's contribution was entirely indirect: stronger PA reduced pausal intrusions, which maintained temporal stability and, through it, reading fluency.
Conclusion: PA appears to influence reading fluency indirectly through sequential, temporal prosodic execution. In syllable-timed languages like Hungarian, sentence-level temporal mechanisms may carry the primary explanatory weight, highlighting that reading development models should account for the specific rhythmic properties of the reader's native language.

articles.title: Correcting misconceptions and shaping preferences about energy with reinforcement learning
articles.authors: Caroline Pioger; Fabien Cerrotti; Wataru Toyokawa; Maël Lebreton; Stefano Palminteri
articles.abstract: Addressing the climate crisis requires citizens to make informed choices about sustainable energy policy, yet public debates are often shaped by inaccurate beliefs about the environmental and health impacts of different energy sources. Misconceptions about key features of energy sources, such as their greenhouse gas emissions, mortality rates, and contribution to electricity production, are particularly dangerous for this debate, as they risk systematically distorting public support for effective decarbonisation strategies. Here we investigate whether a brief reinforcement‑based intervention can correct such misconceptions and influence societal investment preferences. Across seven countries, we reveal systematic misbeliefs, such as overestimating the emissions and mortality of nuclear power and under‑estimating the mortality of biomass, which were corrected by our intervention across all features and countries. Furthermore, correcting beliefs led to shifts in preferences towards objectively cleaner and safer energy mixes, and these changes were consistent across countries. Follow‑up assessments indicated that most of our intervention’s effects were detectable after 14 weeks. These results demonstrate a three‑step actionable pathway, from behavioural feedback, through belief correction, to preference change, and suggest that short, reinforcement‑based interventions could be a scalable tool for improving public decision‑making in climate policy and other domains where misconceptions pollute the debate.

articles.title: The Dimensionality of Misinformation Susceptibility: General Disposition or Domain-Specific Tendencies?
articles.authors: Anton Andersson; Artur Nilsson
articles.abstract: This research investigated the dimensionality of misinformation susceptibility in the form of unwarranted conspiracy theories, pseudoscience, and pseudo-profound bullshit in representative samples of Swedish (N = 2283) and British (N = 3005) adults, through CFA and ESEM with target rotation. The results yielded strong support for weak generality, i.e., substantial correlations across types of misinformation, but little to no support for strong generality, i.e., the pattern of covariances did not suggest a dominant general factor. Splitting the common factor into separate superordinate factors representing different categories of misinformation improved fit. The main results were generally robust across analyses, suggesting that while people may exhibit a general tendency to be susceptible to misinformation, susceptibility also varies across sub-types of misinformation.

articles.title: Sharing biosignals during social interaction modulates psychophysiological  states and perceived interpersonal closeness
articles.authors: Ksenia Egorova; Juan Camilo Avendano-Diaz; Lauri Parkkonen
articles.abstract: Advances in digital technology have made physiological signals such as electrocardiography (ECG) and electrodermal activity (EDA) increasingly accessible, enabling previously covert bodily states to be shared in real time during social exchanges. Recent work, primarily qualitative, suggests that biosignal sharing can modulate social interaction, yet quantitative evidence on its psychophysiological impact remains limited. Here, we investigated whether biosignal sharing during social interaction, and in particular the reciprocity of information exchange, modulates psychophysiological responses. We present data from 18 sex-matched dyads (N = 36) of strangers, whose ECG and EDA were recorded while they engaged in nonverbal face-to-face interaction. Participants shared their heart rate and skin conductance levels (displayed on a monitor) either unidirectionally, bidirectionally, or not at all. We examined the effects of biosignal sharing on indices of autonomic nervous system activity (including RMSSD, skin conductance level, and the number and amplitude of skin conductance responses) and related these measures to psychometric assessments of empathic traits, social interaction anxiety, perceived scrutiny, and interpersonal closeness. Bidirectional biosignal sharing significantly reduced the number of skin conductance responses compared to both face-to-face interaction without sharing and unidirectional sharing. Moreover, greater reductions in sympathetic activation during bidirectional sharing were associated with larger increases in perceived interpersonal closeness. Correlational analyses further indicated that perceived scrutiny was linked to heightened arousal and reduced closeness. Our findings advance the understanding of the physiological and relational impact of biosignal sharing, with direct implications for the design of social computing systems and computer-mediated interactions.

articles.title: Unpacking the Popularity of Online Peer Mental Health Support Groups in Menopause
articles.authors: Emma Bradshaw; Jessica Salvatore; Louise Pendry
articles.abstract: This study connects research on the mental health threats of menopause with research on the effectiveness of online peer support for mental health challenges. Online peer support groups are popular amongst menopausal women, yet the role such groups plays in supporting their psychological well-being has not previously been studied. We used qualitative exploratory research methodology to collate and analyse the experiences of perimenopausal, menopausal, or post-menopausal women who used Facebook to access online peer groups for menopause support. Group members with mental health challenges completed a short questionnaire about their mental health, menopause experiences, and uses/experiences of the group. Participants identified ways in which the group had helped them and positive feelings which had arisen through group use, which had the potential to reduce negative feelings and mental health symptoms experienced during menopause. Additionally, women identified negative impacts of the groups – so they are not a panacea, but should be prominent in the toolbox both for medical professionals and organizations concerned with signposting employees to appropriate support services, given that they are free and easy to access.

articles.title: Effects of Action-Film Versus Nature-Documentary Exposure on  Self-Reported Rational and Experiential Thinking Styles: A Pilot  Experiment
articles.authors: Muhammad Sajjad; Noor Fatima Saeed
articles.abstract:
Whether brief media exposure can shift how people describe their own thinking is poorly 
understood. This pilot experiment tested whether watching an action-film clip changed self-reported 
rational and experiential thinking styles relative to an active comparison condition. Sixteen university 
students were assigned by block randomization to watch either a 40-minute action-film clip (n = 8) or a 
40-minute nature documentary (n = 8). All completed the Rational-Experiential Inventory-40 (REI-40) 
immediately before and after viewing. A 2 (Group) × 2 (Time) mixed ANOVA showed no Group × Time 
interaction for rational ability, rational engagement, or experiential engagement (all p ≥ .270). An 
interaction emerged for experiential ability, F(1, 14) = 4.94, p = .043, η²p = .26, but it did not survive 
correction for four outcomes (Holm-adjusted p = .173). It also reflected a decline in the documentary 
group (−2.88 points) and no change in the action-film group (−0.12), and the subscale had poor internal 
consistency. The groups did not differ at post-test on any subscale, and results were unchanged after 
adjusting for pre-test scores. The study found no evidence that an action-film clip changed self-reported 
thinking styles relative to a nature documentary. With eight participants per group, only very large effects 
could have been detected, so the results are inconclusive about small and moderate effects. Larger, better
matched studies with manipulation checks and behavioral measures of reasoning are needed. 
Keywords: media exposure, thinking styles, Rational-Experiential Inventory, cognitive-experiential self
theory, narrative transportation, pilot experiment

articles.title: From comparison to transformation: studying minds that learn from machines
articles.authors: Francesca Bertacchini; Eleonora Bilotta
articles.abstract: For seventy years, minds and machines have been studied by comparison: can machines model, imitate or outperform us? In bounded domains this comparison has saturated, and machines now produce certified knowledge that no person can inspect; a complete Lean formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem runs to 13.5 million lines. We argue that the object of study must move from the performance gap to the change in minds that learn from machines. We propose Reverse Cognition: a search for faithful, explicitly limited representations through which a person can acquire a certified structure and keep it once the machine is withdrawn. In the public formalization, only 5.7% of the theorems beneath the four steps of the human proof belong to a single step. We define audit criteria for representational routes, machine operations that could make such objects followable, predictions that separate appropriation from offloading, and a study sequence to test them.

articles.title: The Mint Scale: A Fresh Validation of the Multimodal Interoception Questionnaire and Comparison to the MAIA, BPQ and IAS
articles.authors: Dominique Makowski; Ana Neves; Emma Lucy Benn; Maisie Bennett; Giulia Poerio
articles.abstract: Interoception, the sensing of the body's internal state, is an important component of homeostatic and allostatic regulation with wide-ranging implications for mental and physical health, yet its measurement is hindered by tools with conceptual and psychometric issues. To address these limitations, we developed and validated the Multimodal Interoception Questionnaire (Mint). In Study 1 (N=559), a comprehensive item pool using a novel "modality-by-context" framework was generated and then reduced using psychometric network analysis. In Study 2 (N=737), we validated the Mint in an independent sample, establishing its structure,  comparing its predictive power against established interoception questionnaires (MAIA-2, BPQ, IAS), and across a wide range of clinical and cognitive outcomes. This rigorous process yielded a 33-item scale with a stable hierarchical structure comprising three metaclusters (Interoceptive Deficit, Interoceptive Awareness, Visceroception) and 11 distinct facets. The Mint demonstrated superior criterion validity, consistently outperforming existing scales in predicting outcomes tied to altered bodily perception, including alexithymia, ADHD, autism, and somatic symptom clusters. The Mint offers a psychometrically robust and nuanced measure of self-reported interoception that integrates and extends existing scales, providing researchers and clinicians with a practical and readily usable tool to investigate the role of bodily sensations in health and disease.

articles.title: Particularized Truth and Reality Testing in the Algorithmic Era
articles.authors: Daniela Ben Zeev; Dror Oren
articles.abstract:
How can two individuals posing the same question to a conversational model receive different answers, and what are the implications for our understanding of truth and reality testing? The human search for truth has taken various forms: truth as revealed, investigated through science, encountered psychologically, and, today, approached through probability and computation. We distinguish between truth, relative truth, and reality testing, proposing that reality testing relies on an “outside” grounded in objective criteria. Yet conversational models do not merely retrieve information; they formulate a representation of reality within an encounter with a specific inquirer. The user’s input and history participate in shaping the response, such that the “outside” returns tailored to their world. The novelty lies not in algorithmic mediation as such, but in the structural shift in the relationship between subject, representation, and outside.
We propose the concept of Particularized Truth: neither a new ontological category nor a mere adjustment of style, but a form in which a claim about reality becomes present for a specific subject within an algorithmic encounter, influencing content and recommendations. Research on sycophancy provides empirical support for aspects of this adaptive process. Under some conditions, such adaptation may shift the interaction from the demands of the reality principle toward the pleasure principle—the wish that the world offer no resistance. We therefore propose an expansion of reality testing in the AI era, examining how representations are generated and their capacity to diverge from the user’s existing perspective. Reality testing requires an outside, even when the outside has learned to speak our language.

articles.title: Striking the Limits of the Rich-Get-Richer and the Poor-Get-Richer Hypothesis?  Trait Interpersonal Emotion Regulation and its Associations with Instant Messaging Emotional Support and Mental Health in Daily Life
articles.authors: Karen De Raeymaecker; Imke Baetens; Margot Bastin; Martijn Van Heel
articles.abstract: Up until now, the role of dispositions in the psychosocial effects of adolescent instant messaging (IM) remains inconclusive. While the straightforward rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer hypotheses do not allow for nuances about the individual-specific (dis)advantages of offline and online interactions, the literature on the dispositional tendencies for interpersonal emotion regulation shows a more complex picture. In this ecological momentary study (one week, 8 assessments/day), we adopted the rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer framework to test the social and psychological effects of IM with regard to the dispositional tendencies for co-rumination, co-dampening, and co-enhancing in 181 Belgian adolescents (n = 181; Mage = 15.04; 63% women). Adolescents with a higher tendency for co-dampening reported lower mean levels of momentary positive affect. Individuals with a clear tendency for co-enhancing experienced, on average, higher momentary IM emotional support. Regarding the tendency for co-rumination, no significant differences were found. Notably, (dis)advantageous social effects did not go together with similar psychological effects. Unexpectedly, IM behaviors (e.g., IM negative social exchange) were, regardless of the studied outcome and the level of analysis, systematically significant. Overall, this study endorses the importance of the abovementioned dispositional tendencies. Yet, their value was more limited than the rich-get-richer and the poor-get-richer hypotheses predicted.

articles.title: A Momentary Goldilocks Story?  Adolescent Dispositional Traits and their Relationship with Momentary Instant Messaging Social Support and Mental Health
articles.authors: Karen De Raeymaecker; Imke Baetens; Glenn Kiekens; Martijn Van Heel
articles.abstract: Despite the heightened need of connectedness in adolescence, the association between instant messaging (IM) and its psychosocial outcomes remains ambiguous. In line with three existing theories on this topic, ecological momentary assessment (one week, 8 prompts/day) was used to link within-person IM behavior and between-person dispositions with the social outcome perceived IM social support and the psychological outcomes loneliness, depressive feelings, and non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) behavior. Furthermore, the interplay between the two was taken into account. Belgian adolescents (n = 181; Mage = 15.04; 63% women) who reported higher-than-usual IM connection behavior consistently showed better momentary psychosocial outcomes. Robust differences related to the dispositions could only be identified for depressive feelings. Women and participants with higher scores on neuroticism, fear of negative evaluation, social anxiety and distress in new situations, and social comparison orientation proved more vulnerable for these feelings. A tentative association related to loneliness was found for higher neuroticism. Moreover, age (marginally) strengthened the negative association between IM behavior and the outcomes IM social support and depressive feelings. In general, these findings highlight the importance of the perceived message content, the  potential vulnerability of more extreme dispositions, and the value of embedding psychosocial correlates in a developmental framework.

articles.title: Conditional reasoning in preschoolers: The role of context and alternatives
articles.authors: Ebru Evcen; David Barner
articles.abstract: Understanding conditional inferences is fundamental to human reasoning, allowing us to evaluate possibilities and predict outcomes. For instance, the conditional, “If you eat your broccoli, you’ll get a candy” can be interpreted literally, meaning eating broccoli is one way to get a candy, or pragmatically, implying it is the only way. Past studies find school-aged children (ages 7-12) struggle to arrive at literal meanings but, interestingly, compute adult-like, pragmatic interpretations at this age. An important limitation of past research is the lack of testing in contexts that support literal meanings. We conducted two studies to examine whether children can derive literal interpretations when supported by context. We found that preschoolers as young as 4 years old are adult-like in computing literal meanings when they are able to judge that the antecedent is not the only way to bring about the consequent, either because discourse introduces salient alternatives (Exp 1) or because the stated antecedent is not causally related to the consequent (Exp 2). These findings suggest that preschoolers have the logical ability and processing resources required to make conditional inferences when provided with contextual support.

articles.title: Building Connection Through Conversation: Linguistic Convergence and Neural Complexity in Dyadic Interaction
articles.authors: Grace Qiyuan Miao; Zachary P Rosen; Agnieszka Pluta; MATTHEW D. LIEBERMAN; Rick Dale; Yuwei Li
articles.abstract: Interpersonal connection emerges through conversation. Theories of interpersonal communication hold that conversational partners increasingly align in how they express meaning, build on one another’s contributions, and experience connection. Yet how such alignment unfolds during a conversation, and how it relates to the experience of a “good” interaction, remains largely untested. Seventy dyads of previously unacquainted individuals held naturalistic conversations while dual functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recorded neural activity. We measured semantic alignment using convergence entropy and substantive exchange, the number of adjacent turns in which both partners contributed contentful talk. Contrary to a convergence account, dyads broadened their semantic range over time. Subjective experience was predicted not by semantic alignment but by substantive exchange, particularly in shallow-prompt conversations. Neurally, inter-brain synchrony tracked substantive exchange, whereas semantic alignment was reflected in partners’ matched turn-to-turn neural dynamics. First conversations build connection through reciprocal, substantive exchange, with distinct linguistic and neural signatures.

articles.title: What Are Situationships? Characteristics of an Ambiguous Relationship Type
articles.authors: Saffron Marli Costello; William Costello; Andrew G. Thomas; Martin Graff
articles.abstract:
Situationships are an emerging relationship type, yet quantitative research remains limited. Here we examined situationship characteristics and experiences, using sex and sociosexuality as theoretically relevant starting points for understanding individual variation. We conducted an exploratory, cross-sectional survey of 390 adults (68% women; M age = 27.41 years, SD = 8.66) from 48 countries who reported on current, or emotionally significant past, situationships. Participants endorsed proposed situationship characteristics and provided their own open-ended definitions which underwent structured content coding. These analyses informed a working definition of situationships as intimate, relationship-like connections lacking clarity about commitment, relationship status, or future trajectory. Although 56% of participants entered situationships hoping for a relationship, and 55% assumed sexual exclusivity, only 9% of reported past situationships progressed to a committed relationship. Compared with men, women more often emphasised ambiguity in their definitions, perceived greater long-term potential, and expressed stronger hopes for commitment. They also more strongly agreed that they would feel betrayed if their situationship partner saw other people. Relative to the reference sample, both sexes reported more unrestricted sociosexual behaviour, whereas women reported more restricted sociosexual attitudes. This pattern raises questions about incongruence between women’s sexual experiences and preferences, with potential implications for wellbeing. The observed sex differences also motivate future research to examine whether divergent mating goals between partners shape situationship experiences.
Keywords: situationships, romantic relationships, sex differences, sociosexuality

articles.title: Factor Structure of the Auditory-Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire  and Development of a Brief Scale
articles.authors: Zach Hambrick; Elizabeth S. Eberlin; Katharine N. Thakkar
articles.abstract: Nikitova and colleagues’ Auditory and Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire (AVAQ) is the first comprehensive assessment of the type of perceptual abnormalities associated with the schizophrenia spectrum (Nikitova et al., 2019). The primary aim of this study was to investigate the factor structure of the AVAQ and develop a brief version of the scale. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses indicated that the AVAQ is multidimensional, capturing a general factor of perceptual abnormalities, along with more specific types of perceptual abnormalities. Through item-level analyses, we identified 23 items that capture this factor structure. A Brief AVAQ scale consisting of these 23 items exhibited good reliability and convergent validity in two relatively large samples. This scale could be used in both research and clinical practice.

articles.title: Delusion-like content emerges from common-cause inference over semantically disparate observations
articles.authors: Matthew Schafer; Emmett M. Larsen; Kiyohito Iigaya; Guillermo Horga
articles.abstract: Delusions are beliefs with extraordinary content, yet computational accounts of delusions have not explained how this content arises. We propose that extraordinary content emerges when an ordinary mechanism, common-cause inference, is applied to semantically disparate observations. We tested this with large language models (LLMs) by systematically manipulating semantic disparity between observations. Single causes inferred by these models from ordinary observations generally resembled true causes, yet became increasingly delusion-like as observations became more disparate. Observation disparity predicted delusionality, and this relationship could be explained geometrically via semantic analogues of common-cause properties. We further tested this idea in a large corpus of real-world delusions. In cases documenting pre-delusional observations, subsequent delusional beliefs were consistent with what LLMs would infer and exhibited corresponding common-cause properties. Together, our findings identify a computational route through which extraordinary delusion-like content can emerge from ordinary causal inference, and demonstrate its relevance to clinical delusions.

articles.title: Disrupting social media habits: a one-week detox produces enduring reductions in use and automaticity
articles.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Suhaavi Kochhar; Mariek Magdalena Petra Vanden Abeele; Sanne de Wit
articles.abstract: This randomised controlled trial examines if a one-week social media abstinence intervention can reduce social media use by lowering automaticity of and craving for social media use. Participants motivated to reduce their social media use were assigned to an immediate one-week detox (N = 50) or a waitlist control condition (N = 64). Using a combination of smartphone usage logging and weekly surveys, we found that the detox produced significant reductions in social media use (d = 0.51), automaticity (d = 1.10), and craving (d = 0.58) one week post-detox relative to the waitlist group. Exploratory mediation analyses provided suggestive evidence that automaticity partially mediated the detox's effect on social media use. Furthermore, baseline automaticity predicted self-reported vulnerability to slips of action during the detox, i.e. spontaneous attempts to open removed apps. Pooling data from both groups after each had completed the detox (N = 108), we found that the reductions persisted across the three-week follow-up and that social media use remained below baseline at a six-month follow-up in a subsample (N = 46). The detox also shifted participants' subjective relationship with social media, increasing perceived control and reducing self-reported mindlessness, without changing how much they liked it or considered it purposeful. Together, these findings suggest that for those who want to cut back, taking a short break is an effective way to disrupt social media habits and restore a sense of control.

articles.title: Comparing physical literacy scores by sex and movement behaviour distributions across physical literacy profiles among elementary school students: an exploratory study
articles.authors: Henri Moncanis; Pierre-Yves de Müllenheim; Nicolas Hauw
articles.abstract: Current literature supports the idea that physical literacy may serve as a key concept for promoting, in children, physically active lifestyles over the long term. However, in France, few studies have focused on physical literacy levels among children, particularly when it comes to comparing scores between boys and girls. Building on a North American approach, the Canadian Assessment of Physical Literacy Second Edition (CAPL-2) framework provides classification of physical literacy profiles based on the overall physical literacy score across four main dimensions: physical, behavioural, affective, and cognitive. The association between these profiles and relevant indicators of movement behaviour distribution remains unclear in the literature. Therefore, the present exploratory study had two main aims: (i) to compare physical literacy scores by sex; and (ii) to compare, across physical literacy profiles, indicators of movement behaviour distribution (intensity gradient, tendency to spend time at higher intensities, and power-law exponent alpha, sedentary accumulation patterns). Ninety-nine final-year primary school students (Avrillé, Maine-et-Loire, France) were assessed using the CAPL-2. CAPL-2 total scores, multivariate combinations of CAPL-2 domain and item scores by sex, and multivariate combinations of movement behaviour distribution metrics across physical literacy profiles were compared using nonparametric analyses. The results encourage conducting confirmatory studies focusing primarily on sex differences in overall physical literacy and the affective dimension. It also supports conducting studies confirming the ability of physical literacy profiles to reflect the intensity gradient, that is, children's tendency to spend their activity time at higher intensities.

articles.title: CaliGaze: A Validated Webcam Eye-Tracking Framework for Attentional Drift-Diffusion Modeling
articles.authors: Qiang Shen; Qingyan Xiao; Shiguang Fu
articles.abstract: Eye-tracking has become central to process-tracing research in judgment and decision-making, yet access to this paradigm remains constrained by the cost and logistical demands of research-grade infrared systems. We present CaliGaze, an open-source webcam eye-tracking framework that uses geometric iris landmark estimation, individually calibrated piecewise spatial mapping, and a recorded single-eye eyelid-opening validity flag to support ROI-level gaze classification in binary choice experiments. In a within-subject validation study (N = 51), CaliGaze was evaluated against a Tobii Pro Spark infrared eye tracker while participants completed a risky binary choice task with simultaneous dual-system recording. CaliGaze showed strong cross-device agreement in ROI-level dwell proportions and reproduced the core fixation-choice signatures of the task. Both gaze streams consistently supported gaze-dependent over gaze-independent evidence accumulation, and attentional-weighting estimates showed strong cross-device correspondence in between-participant rank ordering. These results suggest that CaliGaze can support ROI-level process tracing and gaze-dependent computational modeling in binary choice tasks, offering a scalable and accessible alternative for decision researchers, with particular potential for large-scale, remote, or resource-limited settings.

articles.title: The influence of attention on visual statistical learning and vice versa: Insights from frequency-based grouping as revealed by EEG frequency tagging
articles.authors: Elena Greatti; Davide Crepaldi
articles.abstract: The human brain readily captures regularities in the environment. It is not clear, however, whether and how this skill—statistical learning—interacts with attention. We addressed this issue by leveraging neural entrainment, the synchronization of brain activity with statistical structure. In Study 1, we asked whether sensitivity to a frequency-based regularity, created by embedding low-frequency items among higher-frequency items, competes for attentional resources with a concurrent task. Participants viewed structured or random visual streams while performing a 3-back color matching task. Neural entrainment emerged only for structured streams, demonstrating sensitivity to the frequency structure. Improvement in the concurrent task, indexed by decreasing response times, unfolded more slowly when structure was present, suggesting that detecting statistical regularities drew attention away from the 3-back color matching task. In Study 2, we tested the reverse connection—whether taxing attention with a more difficult task impairs the neural tracking of statistical structure. We compared entrainment during an easier color-change detection task and a more difficult 3-back color matching task. We observed no detectable effect of attentional load on neural entrainment. These findings reveal an asymmetric relationship between attention and frequency-based statistical learning: detecting structure imposes a modest attentional cost on a concurrent behavioral task, whereas the online neural tracking of regularities appears to be unaffected by increased attentional demands.

articles.title: Metacognitive Monitoring in Naturalistic Translation: a Signal Detection Approach
articles.authors: Aishvarya Raj
articles.abstract:
A novel signal detection approach was applied to translation behavioural data to assess
metacognitive sensitivity for complex, naturalistic tasks, using reformulation behaviour as an
implicit proxy for the confidence response. Existing units of segmentation (Production units
(PU)) were utilised to form trials made up of a Type-1 decision and a Type-2 response. By
using AUROC2, metacognitive sensitivity was estimated for two language-pair corpora under
a lower and upper bound on the response window: an English-Spanish group, where AUROC2
= 0.618 (upper bound) and 0.567 (lower bound), and an English-German group, where
AUROC2 = 0.625 (upper bound) and 0.539 (lower bound). Under the upper bound, estimates
were reproducible across both corpora, agreeing to within 0.007. Individual differences in
metacognitive sensitivity were dissociable from translation accuracy and varied considerably
between individual translators. Overall, reformulation behaviour during the drafting phase
carried information about the accuracy of individual productions, as judged against the
translator’s own post-revision translation, and this information was not reducible to their
overall accuracy.

articles.title: “When AI Can Do the Task, Is Learning Still Worth It and Am I Capable?” Scales for Learning Value and Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI and Links to AI Use and Academic Outcomes
articles.authors: Soheil Behdarvandirad; Maryamsadat Mirpour
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now perform many academic tasks that students were once required to master, raising the question of whether learners still value learning for themselves and feel capable of learning without relying on AI. Available scales mainly focus on AI as the outcome of learning rather than the context of it. This study developed and validated brief scales measuring Learning Value in the Context of AI (LV-AI, the value of personally learning when associated tasks can be performed by AI) and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI (LSE-AI, the appraisal of ability to learn and perform academically without relying on AI) and examined their associations with AI use and academic outcomes (effort expenditure, persistence, GPA). Data were collected from 882 undergraduate students in the U.S. with approximately equal traditional-age and adult learners. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis supported a correlated two-factor structure. Both scales showed acceptable reliability (ω = .81 and .72), discriminant validity from classical task value and self-efficacy, and measurement invariance across student age type. When classical task value, classical self-efficacy, and AI use were controlled, LV-AI and LSE-AI incrementally predicted effort and persistence, but not GPA. Moreover, although AI use showed a significant negative association with academic effort, an exploratory mediation analysis indicated that this association no longer held when learners' LV-AI and LSE-AI were accounted for, with the indirect path carrying over half of the initial association. This highlights the important role these AI-embedded constructs play in preventing the disengagement tendencies.

articles.title: Recruiting families into preventive parenting programs: Messaging responses and participation barriers among Chinese-heritage and White parents
articles.authors: Katie Qintan Lin; Emma Marshall; Danhua Zhu; John W Toumbourou; Elizabeth Westrupp
articles.abstract:
Objective: Preventive parenting programs can reduce child mental health risks, but equitable reach requires effective recruitment. Little is known about how recruitment messaging can engage underserved culturally diverse families while retaining broad population appeal. We compared responses to recruitment messaging and participation barriers among Chinese-heritage and White parents. 
Methods: Parents of children aged 2-5 years (100 Chinese-heritage, 101 White) in English-speaking Western countries were recruited online. Participants rated six parenting program recruitment messages based on the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Goal-Directed Behaviour, Norm Activation Model, their combination, or Chinese cultural values (guan and harmony), and nine participation barriers. Mixed-effects regression models examined participation likelihood, perceived program usefulness, and barrier relevance by ethnicity and message/barrier type. 
Results: Chinese-heritage parents reported lower participation likelihood and perceived program usefulness, and higher average barrier relevance than White parents. Ethnicity-by-message interactions were not significant; descriptively, guan was highest rated among Chinese-heritage parents and Goal-Directed Behaviour among White parents, while the combined behavioural theory message was highly rated across groups. Ethnicity-by-barrier interactions were significant: Chinese-heritage parents rated seven of nine barriers as more relevant compared to White parents. Lack of time was most relevant among Chinese-heritage parents; concern about data security was most relevant among White parents, although its relevance did not differ significantly between groups. 
Conclusions: Findings extend research on cultural adaptation to recruitment, and highlight the need to balance cultural responsiveness with broad appeal while addressing families’ differing barriers to participation.

articles.title: Be a Meditator Today: Testing Identity-Based Message Framing for Meditation in a Digital Field Experiment
articles.authors: Michael Bowen
articles.abstract:
Objectives. Brief in-app messages are commonly used to prompt meditation, but little is known about which message features influence engagement. Drawing on the reasoned action approach and research on self-identity, this study tested whether framing meditation as an identity (“Be a meditator today”) rather than a behavior (“Meditate today”) increases engagement, and whether any effect depends on prior engagement.

Methods. In a randomized field experiment on Spotify, 3,000 U.S. adults who had recently listened to a popular meditation teacher received one of two in-app messages that differed only in identity versus behavior framing. Outcomes were message click-through and listening to the teacher’s content during the treatment period, analyzed by intent to treat. Logistic regression tested moderation by prior listening.

Results. Click-through did not differ between conditions (8.2% vs. 8.2%; difference = −0.05 percentage points, 95% CI [−2.03, 1.92]). Identity framing did not increase listening during the treatment period (Mann–Whitney U = 1,106,605, p = .313; mean difference = 1.26 min, 95% CI [−5.72, 8.24]). Prior listening (median split) did not moderate the effect of framing (interaction OR = 0.93, 95% CI [0.55, 1.56], p = .77).

Conclusions. Identity-based framing did not increase engagement, even among an audience for whom the meditator identity was plausible. Consistent with the reasoned action approach, changing a message’s grammatical form without changing the beliefs it makes salient may offer little leverage over behavior.

articles.title: From Bulking to Cutting: Social Media, Self-Esteem, and Disordered Eating in Young Men
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Bulking and cutting (caloric surplus and restriction) are increasingly common among young men but remain under-researched within disordered eating frameworks. This study examined social media use and self-esteem as predictors, as well as their association with disordered eating and bulking and cutting behaviours. Seventy-six physically active UK men aged 18-25 years (M = 22.07, SD = 2.07) completed online measures of social media use, self-esteem, disordered eating (restraint, eating concern, shape concern, weight concern), and bulking and cutting behaviours. Higher social media use predicted higher eating concern (p = .003), while lower self-esteem predicted higher eating and shape concerns (p = .029, p = <.001). Neither social media use nor self-esteem predicted restraint, bulking, or cutting. Exploratory mediation analyses showed that restraint fully mediated the association between shape concern and cutting behaviour (p = < .001). Social media use and self-esteem appear to relate to specific disordered eating symptoms, whereas bulking and cutting may be more closely linked to restraint processes. These findings support expanding conceptualisations of disordered eating in young men to include muscle-oriented dietary behaviours and their distinct psychological pathways.

articles_hidden.title: Mediators of the link between parental monitoring and youth adjustment: a review of the evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Meghan Dontha; Sophia Helena Blyth; Carolyn L. Foo; Tia C. Chitty; Oscar Gonzalez; William E. Pelham
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: By what mechanisms does parental monitoring affect youth adjustment? This paper
aimed to review every published study that has tested a statistical mediator of
monitoring→adjustment.
Method: We searched for studies that (a) enrolled elementary-, middle-, and/or high-school aged
youth, (b) measured parental monitoring as parent action (vs., e.g., knowledge), and (c) tested a
statistical mediation model linking monitoring to any form of youth adjustment.
Results: 39 papers have tested a mediator of the link from monitoring → adjustment. Most
papers used cross-sectional data only (26 of 39) on typically developing samples (33 of 39). All
papers were non-experimental. Only 1 of 39 papers made a substantial effort to rule out potential
confounding - most adjusted for just a few measured covariates. Across the 39 papers, 79 out of
173 tests of mediation were statistically significant (46%). Of the significant tests, 59 indicated
beneficial effects of monitoring, and 20 indicated detrimental effects of monitoring. There was at
least one statistically significant test for 42 distinct pairs of mediator and outcome, but only 6
mediational chains had been replicated in more than one paper. Effect sizes for single mediators
were typically small (median standardized ab = -0.02) and suggested multiple mediators would
be needed to explain the total effect (median percent mediated = 24%). Of relevance to Stattin
and Kerr’s (2000) classic argument, we found only 1 paper testing whether youth disclosure
mediates the link between monitoring and adjustment.
Conclusion: There are now many published tests of the mediators linking parental monitoring to
youth adjustment. However, few have been replicated, and fewer still have been rigorous. As a
result, the extant evidence can be reconciled with many (if not all) major theories about how
parental monitoring works.

articles_hidden.title: Cannabis Use Disorder and Depressive Symptoms: A within-network resting-state functional connectivity study
articles_hidden.authors: Nora de Bode; Emese Kroon; Jia Hua Hsieh; Francesca Filbey; Janna Cousijn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Cannabis use disorder (CUD) frequently co-occurs with depressive symptoms, yet shared underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the role of depressive symptoms in the relationship between CUD, cannabis use characteristics, and within-network resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) in the Executive Control (ECN), the Salience (SN), the Default Mode (DMN), and the Basal Ganglia (BGN) networks.
Methods: In a pooled sample of 132 CUD participants and 102 controls, we examined the associations of group, depressive symptoms, and their interaction with within-network RSFC. Within the CUD group, we assessed the associations between cannabis use characteristics, depressive symptoms, and RSFC. We also conducted an exploratory, non-preregistered sensitivity analysis in the largest contributing study (n = 187).  
Results: In the full sample and the largest study, depressive symptoms were associated with higher RSFC in the left ECN and interacted with group in the right ECN, showing a positive association between depressive symptoms and RECN RSFC in controls, but not in CUD individuals. The largest study analysis additionally showed lower dorsal SN and higher BGN RSFC in CUD individuals relative to controls. Within the full CUD sample, depressive symptoms were positively associated with anterior SN RSFC among individuals with heavier cannabis use, but negatively among those with lighter use.
Conclusion: CUD, heaviness of cannabis use, and depressive symptoms may concurrently relate to RSFC alterations within distinct networks. Group differences potentially emerge at higher levels of CUD and depression severity. This highlights the importance of accounting for depressive symptoms in neurobiological research on CUD.

articles_hidden.title: How Interchangeable Are Webcam and Infrared Eye-Tracking Data in Educational Science Contexts? A Within-Participant Comparison in the Laboratory and at Home
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Kosel; Christian Hartmann; Tina Seidel
articles_hidden.abstract: Eye tracking is a key method in educational sciences, for example, in studying teachers' professional vision. However, currently used infrared (IR) eye trackers confine research to small laboratory samples. Webcam-based eye tracking could enable large online studies, but its data quality for educational contexts such as classroom video has to be empirically determined. Seventy-nine participants viewed five classroom video vignettes twice, with a webcam-based system (Labvanced) and an IR system (Tobii Pro Spectrum). Webcam recordings took place in the laboratory (n = 45) or at home (n = 34). Webcam precision was markedly worse than IR precision (laboratory medians within fixations: 0.37° vs. 0.12°; dz = 2.97). With identical processing, fixation counts, fixation durations, and saccade amplitudes were not equivalent across systems. A more tolerant webcam threshold equalized fixation counts but not durations, and a noise-robust algorithm reversed the duration difference, so these measures reflect noise rather than viewing behavior. After offset correction, dwell-time distributions on coarse grids agreed across systems (r = .73 for 4 × 4 cells). It rested on regions all viewers attended to; individual deviations from this pattern were reliable within each system but did not correspond across systems. At home, angular precision did not decrease, but the signal was noisier relative to the stimulus, and usability ratings were lower and more variable. Webcam-based eye tracking can thus describe how attention is distributed across dynamic videos at a coarse scale, but neither individual differences in dwell time nor fixation-based measures are currently interchangeable with IR data.

articles_hidden.title: How Predictive Spatial Constraints Shape Object Recognition
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah Lum Smith; Monica S. Castelhano
articles_hidden.abstract: Observers use high-level knowledge to support object recognition, including expectations about object locations. However, these expectations are not uniform: some objects have precise object-location priors, whereas others have more flexible spatial distributions. Across two experiments collected in 2024-2025, we examined how the precision of object-location priors shapes object processing by manipulating spatial certainty and object placement within scenes. Experiment 1 used an online two-alternative forced-choice recognition task, and Experiment 2 used a gaze-contingent paradigm to examine processing across fixations. Recognition accuracy and sensitivity showed a significant interaction between spatial certainty and placement: high-certainty objects benefited from expected placement and were impaired by unexpected placement, whereas low-certainty objects showed weaker placement effects. In contrast, eye movement measures in Experiment 2 showed broad effects of placement, but no interaction with spatial certainty. These findings suggest contextual prediction in scenes is graded, object-specific, and temporally distinct across visual processing and recognition.

articles_hidden.title: Experiential value neglect in hybrid choice is robust to learning and representational manipulations.
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline Pioger; Basile Garcia; Maël Lebreton; Stefano Palminteri
articles_hidden.abstract: In decision‑making, option values can arise from past experiences with rewards and punishments (experiential) or from explicit descriptions of outcomes and probabilities (descriptive). While most studies have examined experiential and descriptive options separately, real‑world decisions, such as deciding between a restaurant we visited before and one known through online reviews, often entail choosing between the two. Recently, Garcia et al. (2023) revealed that experiential options are systematically neglected in such hybrid choices. Yet, the cause of this experiential neglect remains unknown. To test whether this phenomenon results from representational differences between experiential and descriptive options, we manipulated the learning architecture, test‑phase feedback, stimulus format, and feedback format over five experiments (n = 375). Participants showed reduced sensitivity to experiential losses relative to gains. Importantly, experiential neglect persisted across all conditions, eliminating these hypotheses as explanations of this phenomenon. Rather, we propose that neglect may stem from retrieval‑based uncertainty in experiential valuation. Together, these findings provide evidence for a cognitive constraint on the integration of experiential and described values in decision‑making.

articles_hidden.title: Benchmarking the Double-Entry Intraclass Correlation as an Index of the Similarity between Correlation Profiles
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Blötner
articles_hidden.abstract: To infer whether the test scores subjected to analyses tap into the same construct (or opposite ones), measured as the similarity between sets of correlations with other variables, researchers often use the Double-Entry Intraclass Correlation (ICCDE). Importantly, the ICCDE has been developed as an index of the similarity between profiles consisting of unbounded coefficients (e.g., profiles of personality features), whereas the correlation metric conveys a series of challenges to the applicability of the ICCDE. Using simulation studies, this research benchmarked the applicability of the ICCDE to correlation profiles under various conditions regarding characteristics of the correlation profiles subjected to analysis. More specifically, equality versus inequality of the patterns of correlation trajectories (shape), levels of variance of the compared correlation profiles (scatter), and mean levels of the profiles (elevation) were manipulated along with the level of variance within the correlation profiles. Simulation results indicate that ICCDE values can be strongly influenced by profile shape and restricted within-profile variance. These findings suggest that conclusions about similarity between correlation profiles may depend on characteristics of the compared profiles and have important implications for evaluating jingle and jangle fallacies.

articles_hidden.title: Hunger and Concentration in Daily Life: Inter-Individual Differences and Eating-Related Variation but No Robust Average Association
articles_hidden.authors: Christoph Bamberg; Julia Reichenberger; Jens Blechert
articles_hidden.abstract: Momentary reductions in concentration may affect daily functioning. In addition to external distractors, bodily signals might divert attention from ongoing tasks. Hunger might not only signal short dips in energy supply but also trigger distracting interoceptive sensations. We focus on hunger as a frequent sensation that is regularly regulated through food intake and therefore may display a complex relation to concentration. To test the relation between hunger and concentration, 64 participants in an experience sampling study reported their momentary concentration, hunger, and food intake six times daily for four weeks. Using Bayesian multilevel within between models, we assessed the hunger concentration association and, in exploratory analyses, whether this relation differed depending on prior food intake. We found no robust average hunger concentration association, with a Bayes Factor supporting the absence of a systematic population level within participant association. At the same time, the association varied considerably between individuals. Prior food intake did not clearly change the association overall. In exploratory meal-specific-analyses, more negative hunger concentration associations were estimated after breakfast and lunch compared with assessments without the respective meal. Thus, the momentary hunger concentration relation in daily life was characterised by considerable inter-individual differences and possible dependence on specific meal contexts. These findings suggest that everyday concentration may be shaped less by hunger per se than by individual differences and the context in which hunger occurs.

articles_hidden.title: PraBat: An item response theory-based test battery to assess individual differences in pragmatic abilities in preschool children from different cultural backgrounds
articles_hidden.authors: Chiara Carraro; Paula Waffen; Pelin Küçükerdoğan; Elif Ayça Yiğit; Mayurbhai Jakharabhai Odedra; Henriette Zeidler; Aylin C. Küntay; Bahar Koymen; Daniel Haun; Manuel Bohn
articles_hidden.abstract: Pragmatic abilities allow us to use and comprehend language in interaction. The assessment of individual differences in pragmatic abilities, both within and across cultural settings, is crucial to understanding how they develop. However, tools with good psychometric properties that suit this purpose are lacking. The current study describes the creation of a test battery assessing individual differences in 3- to 6-year-old children from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds. The battery is implemented as a tablet-based game, administrable both online and in person. Children are prompted by a character with one or multiple utterances and respond by selecting a picture among three options on a screen. An initial larger item pool was piloted in Germany and Kenya to ensure the items’ cross-cultural adaptability. We then used item response modeling on a sample of 713 German children to select items that varied in difficulty and fit the Rasch model. The so-constructed 19-item battery shows excellent model fit, test-retest reliability and convergent validity. The way the battery was created allows for easy cross-cultural adaptation, easy administration and scoring, thereby addressing an important gap in the developmental study of the interplay between social cognition and language. All materials and code are freely accessible to interested researchers. The task can be used via the following website: https://devpsy.web.leuphana.de/prabat/.

articles_hidden.title: Testing the Speed–Duration Link: Perceptual Equalization of Motion Speed Reduces the Foveal Duration Bias
articles_hidden.authors: Hakan Karsilar; Hedderik van Rijn; Sebastiaan Mathot
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual processing varies systematically with eccentricity: Stimuli in the periphery are perceived as slower, lower in contrast, and shorter in duration compared with foveal stimuli. Whether these asymmetries reflect a single underlying mechanism, such that removing one asymmetry eliminates others, or partly distinct mechanisms remains unknown. We tested this question for perceived motion speed and duration, both underestimated in the periphery, by asking whether perceptually equalizing motion speed across the visual field eliminates or reduces the foveal duration bias. In a two-phase design, each participant's peripheral speed bias was first measured at two eccentricities (approximately 11° and 22°). Participants then compared the durations of foveal and peripheral random dot kinematograms (100–1,600 ms) under physical or perceptual speed equality. The calibration showed robust peripheral speed underestimation at both eccentricities, increasing with distance from fixation. Under physical speed equality, the foveal stimulus was judged to last longer than the peripheral one. Critically, perceptual speed equalization reduced this foveal duration bias by approximately 60%, and this reduction was larger for participants whose calibrated speed correction was larger, consistent with a dose–response relationship. However, a significant residual bias persisted even after perceptual speed equalization. These findings suggest that asymmetries between foveal and peripheral vision do not reflect a single underlying mechanism, but rather reflect a number of partly distinct yet related mechanisms that operate on different features, in this case motion speed and duration.

articles_hidden.title: Bridging brain structure and function: Structural-functional brain network coupling and frontal midline theta connectivity in general intelligence
articles_hidden.authors: Henrike Maria Jungeblut; Mareike Hülsemann; Erhan Genç; Anna-Lena Schubert
articles_hidden.abstract: Structural connectivity (SC) and functional connectivity (FC), as well as their alignment (SC-FC coupling), may underlie individual differences in general intelligence. We hypothesized that intelligence emerges from optimized SC-FC coupling and additional processes, namely the task-dependent rapid regulation of FC. To test this hypothesis, we examined MRI-derived SC-FC coupling and EEG-derived midfrontal theta FC dynamics as complementary predictors of intelligence within a latent variable framework. We used a sample of 215 healthy adults (113 females) aged 18–40 years who underwent extensive cognitive ability testing and completed a conceptually similar cued task-switching task during EEG and functional MRI acquisition. Although we found no evidence for a broad association between whole-brain SC-FC coupling and intelligence, an exploratory analysis contrasting functional contexts revealed one for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling computed from task-evoked FC. Specifically, higher coupling predicted higher general intelligence, β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.09, 0.47]. Regarding midfrontal theta connectivity, we found no evidence for an association with intelligence at a preregistered electrode (Fz). However, an exploratory analysis of a broader electrode cluster revealed a temporally specific effect, β = 0.36, 95% CI [0.05, 0.67], suggesting that intelligence may rely on flexible modulation of FC across successive stages of information processing. In a combined model, the two connectivity-based predictors showed no substantial correlation with each other, r = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.25], but both remained significant predictors of intelligence, β = 0.26, 95% CI [0.07, 0.45] for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling and β = 0.22, 95% CI [0.06, 0.39] for late midfrontal theta connectivity. Together, both predictors explained 12.7% of variance in intelligence differences. These findings highlight that the connectivity–intelligence association may be spatially and temporally specific, while emphasizing that intelligence relies on multiple connectivity mechanisms spanning the brain’s structure and function.

articles_hidden.title: The Curse of Dimensionality: How Does it Affect Dynamical Systems Research in Clinical Psychology?
articles_hidden.authors: Jingmeng Cui
articles_hidden.abstract: The dynamical systems approach is gaining attention across many subfields of clinical psychology. Although the systems are assumed to involve many variables, theoretical and methodological work in this field often relies on low-dimensional stability landscapes, creating potential mismatches. In this article, I discuss how high-dimensional stability landscapes may challenge intuitions derived from low-dimensional landscapes, put forward a potential solution based on sufficient low-dimensional descriptions, and propose a future research agenda centered on dimensionality reduction approaches that emphasize preserving information about stability and transitions.

articles_hidden.title: There is no time for time: a critical review of temporality within social representations theory
articles_hidden.authors: Mirella de Falco; Luciano Moreira; Orsolya Vincze; Mauro Sarrica
articles_hidden.abstract:
Time is foundational to social life, yet Social Representations Theory has often treated it as the background against which representations change, rather than as a dimension of meaning-making in its own right. This theoretical review distinguishes processual dynamics (how representations emerge, stabilize, circulate, and transform) from temporality: how past, present, and future are socially and symbolically constituted. From here, it examines structural, dialogical, sociodynamic, and genetic approaches in order to trace how these traditions have engaged with the past through narratives, memories, and histories, and with the future through projects, expectations, and anticipations. The review shows that all four traditions contain temporal assumptions, but that the field has developed fuller accounts of how the past organizes the present than of how possible futures orient collective life. Drawing together conceptual resources already present within the theory, we propose a re-temporalization organized around four components: temporal contents, representational processes, projects, and projections. This agenda treats time as symbolically constructed, experientially lived, normatively encoded, and politically distributed. It enables research to examine how groups negotiate temporal pace, direction, reversibility, and legitimacy, and how unequal capacities to define the past and the future shape representational life. Re-temporalizing SRT therefore deepens the theory’s concern with common-sense knowledge by linking continuity and transformation to the politics of memory and anticipation.

KEYWORDS:  social representations, temporality, collective memory, anticipation, dialogicality, meaning-making

articles_hidden.title: Interpersonal heterogeneity and the presentation and course of mental disorders: A systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Marije aan het Rot; Svenja Heinrichs; Zohra Buring; Nives Mandic; Jacqueline Peters; Annelieke Roest
articles_hidden.abstract: In the past two decades, research has indicated that variation in the course of mental disorders may be partially explained by interpersonal heterogeneity. Patients with interpersonal different styles can have variable outcomes even when they do not differ in pre-treatment symptom presentation or psychiatric diagnosis. This phenomenon is known as interpersonal pathoplasticity. In this paper we present the results of a systematic review of 19 studies conducted in adult patients with DSM-IV Axis I mental disorders that (a) used the Inventory of Interpersonal Problems to identify subgroups of patients with similar interpersonal styles, and (b) compared these interpersonal subgroups in terms of demographic and clinical characteristics (e.g., age, symptom severity) and course over time (e.g., therapeutic alliance development). Across diagnostic categories, we found few differences between subgroups in demographics and in clinical presentation. At the same time, there were subgroup differences in the course of mental disorder. Specifically, having a warm-submissive interpersonal style tended to be more favourable for treatment than having a cold-submissive or cold-dominant style, in support of interpersonal pathoplasticity. This phenomenon has transdiagnostic potential in clinical practice, since between-person variation in interpersonal style provides opportunities for improving and tailoring treatment. However, our review primarily included studies on patients diagnosed with anxiety and mood disorders. To find additional evidence for interpersonal pathoplasticity, future studies should assess interpersonal heterogeneity in patients with other mental disorders and examine its relation to the course of these disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Thought for food: Individual differences in how food decisions are made
articles_hidden.authors: Caitlin Lloyd; Zarrar Shehzad; Janet Schebendach; Akram Bakkour; Alice M Xue; Naomi Assaf; Rayman Jiliani; B. Timothy Walsh; Daphna Shohamy; Joanna Steinglass
articles_hidden.abstract: Daily food decisions accumulate to impact physical health, but making choices consistent with longer-term health goals can prove challenging. Prior research has focused predominantly on dampening preferences for highly palatable foods, or exerting self-control, as the mechanism for healthier food choices. Consequently, the range of cognitive strategies for healthy eating, and how they vary with demographic characteristics, remains unclear. Here, a large US sample (N = 1,052) completed an online food rating and choice task, and demographic and eating behavior questionnaires. Participants rated foods across 17 dimensions, which were reduced to three underlying core food attributes by factor analysis: Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami (capturing food savoriness). All attributes influenced food choices. A multi-attribute drift diffusion model quantified distinct yet latent choice processes, including the deliberation required prior to making a choice. The influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami on choice varied across the study population. Women, individuals endorsing higher levels of eating restraint, and individuals with lower BMI selected subjectively healthier foods more frequently. Making subjectively healthier choices was not dependent only on engaging self-control. Rather, individuals making subjectively healthier choices perceived subjectively healthier foods as tastier. In addition, individuals endorsing high levels of eating restraint required less deliberation when making choices, suggesting more automatic decision-making. These findings suggest multiple routes to making healthier food choices and question the narrative that food tastiness must be sacrificed to support physical health.

articles_hidden.title: Reappraisal and Acceptance Differentially Shape Psychomotor Performance
articles_hidden.authors: David Brian Rompilla; Takashi Yamauchi; Claudia M. Haase; Emily Villalobos; Giovanni Jabbour
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotion regulation strategies such as reappraisal and acceptance can influence not only emotional experience, but also subsequent performance on cognitive tasks. Some findings suggest that regulation impair subsequent performance by taxing executive-control resources, whereas others suggest that regulation can enhance performance. These mixed findings indicate that the effects of regulation on later performance depend not only on the effort a strategy requires, but also on how it shapes the processes that turn thoughts into actions. To test this idea, we used mouse-cursor tracking to examine the extent to which the two strategies influence action: motor preparation, execution, and selection. Across two studies, participants watched sad film clips while using either positive reappraisal or emotional acceptance in within-person blocks. Participants subsequently completed mouse-tracking choice-reaching versions of the Attention Network (Study 1; N = 164) or Stroop task (Study 2; N = 152). Across both studies, participants responded more quickly after reappraisal than after acceptance, without reduced accuracy. This response-time advantage emerged primarily after movement began (motor execution) and was not fully accounted for by emotional experience, perceived implementation demands, or movement vigor. These findings suggest that reappraisal and acceptance differentially shape not only how people feel, but also how they act.

articles_hidden.title: Worry is underpinned by persistence in searching uninformative avenues
articles_hidden.authors: Alexis An Yee Low; Karl Friston; Michael Moutoussis
articles_hidden.abstract: Worry is common both in mental health and distress. What, then, distinguishes pathological worry? We hypothesized that what characterizes pathological worry is excessive internal search that fails to resolve uncertainty; i.e., is uninformative. In an information sampling paradigm, increased sampling was predicted both by trait (p = .018) and—more powerfully—state worry (p < .001). An information-poor environment significantly increased sampling in high worriers (p < 0.001, CrI 1.1% inside Region of Practical Equivalence defined as <0.2 SD), but not low worriers (p = 0.480, CrI 68.2% in ROPE). Crucially, this increase in sampling in high worriers did not increase their accuracy (CrI 97.5% inside ROPE). A ‘sampling until success’ heuristic was identified as a driver. Stimulus uncertainty and aversiveness had similar effects on sampling and worry, increasing both (p < 0.001). Persistent searching—in the face of irreducible uncertainty—may therefore be a key mechanism behind worry, differentiating high from low worrying.

articles_hidden.title: Seeing without understanding? The protracted development of children’s ability to use third-party attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation
articles_hidden.authors: Shengyi Wu; Laura Schulz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Although children react poorly to inattentive adults, they may do so because their needs are not being met rather than because they understand that the adult is distracted by something else. Given third-party observations, we find no evidence that children under six expect others to prefer attentive to distracted social partners (Exps 1-3), have preferences themselves (Exp 4), or select interventions likely to engage a partner’s attention (Exp 5). This is not due to task demands: Four- and five-year-olds have no difficulty recognizing that people prefer social
partners who fulfill (versus override) their desires (Exp 6); using differences in visual attention to infer what others know (Exp 7), or distinguishing attentive and distracted social partners (Exp 8). The results suggest that young children may understand attention primarily as visual attention rather than cognitive engagement, and thus fail to appreciate its social value.

articles_hidden.title: Distinct yet coupled hemispheric codes for foveal visual processing
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda K Robinson; Tijl Grootswagers; Sophia M. Shatek; Marlene Behrmann; Thomas A. Carlson
articles_hidden.abstract: Perceiving the world feels effortless, yet it is accomplished by two hemispheres that do not process visual information in the same way. Whether this involves distinct processing cascades, tight hemispheric coupling, or something in between has fundamental implications for understanding the emergence of coherent perception from divided processes. Images presented to the fovea project to both hemispheres, offering an opportunity to isolate intrinsic hemispheric differences in visual coding. Here, we used electroencephalography and neural decoding methods to investigate the dynamics of foveal visual processing in the left and right hemispheres. Human participants (N = 20; 15 females, 5 males) viewed images of objects, faces and words in rapid sequences while performing an orthogonal task. We found different trajectories of visual coding within the left and right hemispheres, and these differences were characterised by distinct featural biases in each hemisphere, with a particular left bias for rectilinearity and right bias for colour. Yet, despite encoding visual information differently, the left and right hemispheres appear to converge on a shared representation. The results provide new insights into hemispheric dynamics underlying visual perception and the complementary roles of the left and right hemispheres in processing visual information.

articles_hidden.title: Why curricula help some learners and not others
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammed Amara; Christopher Summerfield
articles_hidden.abstract: Curriculum learning, the deliberate ordering of learning experiences, is central to how humans and animals learn, yet its benefits in neural networks are inconsistent. We argue that curricula succeed when they prevent or correct early commitments that might otherwise predispose learners to underfit or overfit to training data. Early experience can lead learners to overlook relevant information, or to rely on irrelevant details that do not generalise well. Curricula help by preventing these mistakes or making them easier to correct. Their benefits diminish when learners have spare capacity or suitable representations, and curricula can even harm learning when early experience establishes patterns that later experience cannot build on. The main source of curriculum benefit, thus, is helping learners `unlearn' overly simple or overly complex solutions.

articles_hidden.title: Interoceptive sensibility tracks confidence, not detection, even without breathing along: five samples with a respiratory change-detection task
articles_hidden.authors: Norman A. S. Farb; Kyle Logie; Rose Amir Pour
articles_hidden.abstract: The Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (MAIA) measures adaptive interoceptive sensibility (attention to the body and how one appraises it) and predicts mental health; how that disposition shows up during a bodily task has rarely been tested. We asked whether MAIA scores predict accuracy, confidence or their coupling in the Breath Change Awareness Task, in which participants breathe along with a visual pacer, report whether its pace changed and rate confidence on every trial. Across five samples (N = 687; in Study 5, a respiratory belt confirmed breathing along in 145 of 170 recorded participants), MAIA scores predicted mean confidence (metacognitive bias) in every sample (pooled r = .27, 95% CI [.17, .37]), including Study 5’s preregistered test (r = .26 [.13, .38]; Breath blocks only, r = .26). They were not positively related to perceptual sensitivity (how well changes were detected) or to metacognitive sensitivity, how well confidence tracked accuracy: pooled, positive relations of r = .10 or more were ruled out for both. Study 5’s preregistered detection-threshold null, a stricter criterion, was not established (BF₀₁ = 2.2, below the required 3). In Study 5, the association held with self-esteem, self-doubt, alexithymia and affect controlled. It was also present with vision alone (following the pacer by eye without breathing along), which should weaken a body-based link: r = .22 [.01, .41], with no detectable difference from breathing along (.20). During sensory discrimination, adaptive sensibility showed up as confidence, independent of accuracy and present even without breathing along.

articles_hidden.title: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Participation and Mental Health Among Combat Veterans with Service-Connected Disabilities: A Single-Arm Longitudinal Pilot Study
articles_hidden.authors: Jack Ryan Kaufman; Wyatt R. Evans; Robert W. Haley; C. Munro Cullum
articles_hidden.abstract: Combat veterans experience higher incidences of depression, anxiety, and PTSD, along with challenges adjusting to life post-discharge, but have been under-served by traditional mental health treatments. Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu has emerged as potentially therapeutic for combat veterans, although empirical support is lacking. A single-arm pre-post pilot study was used to evaluate seven psychosocial outcomes among participants from the We Defy Foundation program (N = 40; 87.5% male; Mage = 41.1, SD = 5.8). Primary outcomes were self-reported post-traumatic stress severity (PTSD Checklist for DSM-5; PCL-5), depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7; GAD-7), and military-to-civilian transition difficulty (Military to Civilian Questionnaire; M2CQ). Secondary outcomes included Self- Efficacy (General Self-Efficacy Scale; GSE), Functional Disability (World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule; WHODAS 2.0), and Life Satisfaction (Satisfaction with Life Scale; SWLS). Assessments were completed at baseline (T0; n = 40), 3 months (T3; n = 34), and 6 months (T6; n = 23). Results revealed high symptom scores at baseline, with significant improvements in the four primary outcomes at both T3 (Cohen’s dz = 0.52–0.63) and T6 (dz = 0.84–1.04) and seven of eight remained significant under Bonferroni correction. GSE and SWLS improved significantly at T3, and SWLS and WHODAS at T6.
