These preliminary findings suggest that BJJ participation may be associated with positive mental health improvements for the veteran population and provide a basis for future controlled studies investigating similar, complementary and alternative approaches.

articles_hidden.title: Gambling in Disguise? A Mixed-Method Examination of Prediction Market Users, Event Preferences, Motives, and Problem Gambling
articles_hidden.authors: Curtis Wagter; Maya Thulin; Philip Newall; Danielle Shinbine; Nalan Guney; Joshua B. Grubbs; Hyoun Soo Kim
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and Aims: Prediction markets have exploded in popularity since a 2024 US court case concluded they should be regulated as financial products, even when used to wager on sport event outcomes. This study therefore explored the convergence of prediction markets and traditional forms of gambling, in particular sports betting. Specifically, we explored whether higher rates of prediction market use would associate with demographic (i.e., age, sex, income, education) and psychological (i.e., impulsivity, financially focused self-concept, psychological distress, problematic alcohol/cannabis use) predictors of problem gambling, alongside direct measures of problem gambling (e.g., Problem Gambling Severity Index [PGSI], Gambling Fallacies Measure [GFM], and Positive Play Scale [PPS]). Participants’ motivations for using prediction markets were obtained via free-text responses.
Methods: Valid data were obtained from a preregistered online cross-sectional study of 938 prediction market users via Prolific in late 2026. A Cochran’s Q test and a z-test explored whether most participants used prediction markets for sports betting and also engaged with conventional gambling products. Ordinal logistic models explored whether higher rates of self-reported prediction market use correlated with demographic, psychological, and gambling predictors of interest. Qualitative inductive content analysis explored participants’ motivations.
Results: As hypothesised, sports contracts were the most popular (81.2%), which was significantly greater than the next most popular category of financial events (55.2%,p<.001). A significant majority of prediction market users also engaged in traditional gambling, (84%;z=20.83,p<.001). As hypothesised, younger age (OR=1.02,p=.048) and being male (OR=1.39, p=.048) were associated with greater prediction market frequency. However, income was not (LRχ²(7)=13.49, p=.061). Being more educated was significantly associated with greater prediction market frequency overall (LRχ²(4)=11.85,p=.025); although no individual category differed from its reference group. As hypothesised, higher scores on four out of five facets of impulsivity (x2(1)=8.25-22.67,ps<.005), higher financially focused self-concept (x2(1)=13.02,p<.001), higher psychological distress (x2(1)=4.11,p<.001), and higher problematic alcohol (x2(1)=15.42,p<.001) and cannabis use (x2(1)=15.71,p<.001) were all associated with greater prediction market use, as was higher PGSI (x2(1)=93.30,p<.001), lower PPS (x2(1)=32.99-65.09,p<.001), but lower GFM was contrastingly not (x2(1)=3.84,p=.050). Participants most commonly reported using prediction markets to win money (52.54%), and reported using them over conventional sportsbooks due to better user-interfaces (36.58%).
Conclusion: US-based prediction market users fit many hallmark characteristics of conventional gambling users, questioning prediction markets’ regulation as financial products.

articles_hidden.title: Where and When to Look: How Expertise and Mental Fatigue Shape Visual Exploration in a Football Task
articles_hidden.authors: Aurélien DEHORNE; Guillaume Hacques; Téo Lepine; Riccardo Palumbo; Giovanni Pezzulo; Pierpaolo Iodice
articles_hidden.abstract: Skillful performance requires picking up information at the right time to both accurately perform ongoing action and search for subsequent ones. The current experiment aimed to compare the visual exploratory activity  (VEA)  of  skilled  (n  =  23)  and  novice  (n  =  21)  players  in  a  football-based  dual  task  scenario  that required to manage competing visual demands for ball manipulation and environmental scanning. Skilled players performed the task faster than novices and showed a more proactive VEA: they spent more time looking at cues related to future passing opportunities while novices looked more at cues related to ball reception. In addition, skilled players made longer scanning movements before receiving the ball, but they did  not perform  significantly  more  head  movements  than  novices. Under  mental  fatigue,  skilled participants preserved their VEA patterns but required longer visual fixations, suggesting a reduced rate of information processing. These findings suggest that expertise in VEA is characterized by the efficient allocation of visual attention rather than merely its quantity.

articles_hidden.title: No convincing evidence for prospective effects between work engagement, burnout, and personality traits: A reassessment of Fukuzaki and Iwata (2027)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Filippa Folke; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Fukuzaki and Iwata concluded, based on analyses with cross-lagged panel models, prospective effects between work engagement, burnout, and personality traits. However, significant cross-lagged parameters do not by themselves establish genuine prospective influence because similar estimates may arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Fukuzaki and Iwata, we examined whether their conclusions were robust across several defensible analytic specifications. The pattern of results depended strongly on analytic choice: some models suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or null effects. When estimates from all specifications were combined using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. Accordingly, the available evidence does not provide a firm basis for concluding that work engagement, burnout, and personality traits exert reciprocal prospective influences on one another. In line with multiverse-analysis recommendations, conclusions should be drawn from the collective pattern across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than from a single model.

articles_hidden.title: Equanimity and Eating-Disorder Vulnerability: Dissociating Psychological Dispositions from Approach–Avoidance Biases
articles_hidden.authors: Nassim Elimari; Claire El Jor; Yoann Julliard; Yoann Durand; Quentin Hallez; Catherine Juneau; Valentin Flaudias; Rebecca Shankland
articles_hidden.abstract: Equanimity, a regulatory quality cultivated through mindfulness practices, refers to the capacity to maintain a balanced mental stance toward pleasant and unpleasant experiences without being automatically driven toward attachment or avoidance. Although theoretically expected to weaken the influence of evaluation on behavior, empirical evidence linking equanimity to observable behavioral dynamics remains limited. The present study examined associations between equanimity, eating-disorder vulnerability, and automatic approach–avoidance tendencies toward food cues. Participants (N = 215) completed self-report measures of equanimity, eating-disorder risk, mindful eating, self-compassion, experiential avoidance, and body acceptance. A subset of 183 participants additionally completed a food-specific approach/avoidance task using stimuli varying in hedonic value. At the dispositional level, equanimity was associated with lower eating-disorder vulnerability and experiential avoidance, and greater self-compassion, body acceptance, and mindful eating. These associations were largely driven by the even-minded state of mind facet of equanimity, whereas hedonic independence showed weaker, more circumscribed relationships with eating- and body-related variables. Behavioral analyses revealed faster avoidance of low-hedonic than high-hedonic food cues, but neither equanimity nor its facets predicted reaction times or moderated hedonic effects on approach/avoidance dynamics. These findings suggest that while equanimity is associated with reduced eating-disorder vulnerability at the trait level, its regulatory role may not manifest in the earliest motor expressions of food-related action tendencies. Instead, equanimity may primarily influence later stages of regulation, such as the interpretation, tolerance, or behavioral management of emerging impulses. However, this interpretation warrants further exploration in experienced meditators, as equanimity in the general population may differ from that cultivated through prolonged contemplative practice.

articles_hidden.title: Near-Death Experiences and Near-Death-Like Experiences: A Comparative Synthesis and Implications for Their Interpretation
articles_hidden.authors: Patrizio Tressoldi
articles_hidden.abstract: Near-death experiences (NDEs) are most often reported in association with physiologically life-threatening events such as cardiac arrest or coma, but phenomenologically similar reports, near-death-like (NDE-like) experiences, also arise in the absence of a life threat, for example during syncope, deep meditation, hypnosis, and psychedelic states. This synthesis reviews the evidence on whether the phenomenology, psychological correlates, and aftereffects of NDEs differ from those of NDE-like experiences. Comparing the largest retrospective survey, a mixed-methods online study, and a within-person psychedelic comparison, consistently indicate broad overlap in core features across contexts. At the same time, encounters with deceased persons or spiritual entities were reported in 34.7% NDE accounts and none of 25 NDE-like accounts in one exploratory study, and a single-case comparison found life review, encounters with the deceased, and a threshold or point of no return present only in the NDE. However, no study was designed to test equivalence, samples were largely self-selected and retrospective, and formal measurement-invariance testing of the instruments in use across etiologies is still lacking. These constraints caution against concluding phenomenological identity. The implications of this evidence for neurophysiological, psychological, evolutionary, and metaphysical interpretations are analyzed, and priorities for prospective, preregistered, adequately powered research are outlined.

articles_hidden.title: Why the Mix Matters - Exploring the Dynamics of Polysubstance Use
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Uhl; Anastasiya Bunina; Birgit Ursula Stetina
articles_hidden.abstract: A widespread form of recreational drug use is known as polysubstance use, which involves consuming two or more psychoactive substances within a short period of time. In addition to the desired effects, such as intensifying or prolonging the high, or counteracting unpleasant effects, polysubstance use also entails risks. To provide polysubstance users with user-centered measures to support health promotion and safer-use, a differentiated understanding of the diverse forms of this consumption practice is required. In an online cross-sectional study, recreational drug users (N= 649) were asked about sociodemographic data and their consumption behavior, with a particular focus on polysubstance use. A hierarchical cluster analysis was performed to identify different types of polysubstance users. The clusters obtained were then tested for diversity using chi-square tests. The cluster analysis revealed three polysubstance use groups that differed in the frequency of mixed use, underlying motivations, and the presence of risk-minimizing strategies. The study showed that consumers who use multiple substances do not constitute a homogeneous group and differ in various characteristics. Taking these individualities and diversities into account must serve as the basis for health promotion to address consumers in a targeted manner.

articles_hidden.title: Confirmatory feedback adds little to serial dependence, whereas error feedback reverses it
articles_hidden.authors: Yael Shamir-Bercovich; Shir Angel; Aihua Chen; ADAM ZAIDEL
articles_hidden.abstract: Perceptual decisions are shaped not only by current sensory input but also by recent experience. Serial dependence exposes an internal brain process that biases current decisions toward previous ones, even in the absence of feedback about their correctness. When available, feedback on one’s choices is an external factor that also shapes subsequent decisions. However, how correct- and incorrect-choice feedback separately affect choice-history biases relative to no feedback, and how these effects vary across individuals and modalities, remains unclear. Here, we compared the effects of serial dependence with or without trial-by-trial feedback on perceptual decisions regarding vestibular or visual self-motion stimuli, and examined how they relate to autistic traits. Seventy healthy adults performed a two-alternative forced-choice heading discrimination task with visual or vestibular cues (separately), under two conditions: with feedback indicating whether each choice was correct or incorrect, and without feedback. Without feedback, significant choice repetition was seen in both modalities. Surprisingly, on average correct-choice feedback did not enhance the choice repetition effect; rather it remained similar in magnitude. By contrast, incorrect-choice feedback led to a large, opposite effect – choice switching – which was stronger for vestibular cues. Thus, only error signals, not confirmatory signals, substantially modulated serial dependence. Choice repetition in the no-feedback vestibular condition correlated significantly with autistic traits. This relationship was not observed when feedback was provided. The similarity in choice repetition following correct-choice feedback vs. no feedback was more pronounced in individuals with high autistic traits, and suggests that positive serial dependence (without feedback) may reflect an internal assumption that one’s decisions were mostly correct.

articles_hidden.title: The built environment and mental health: a neurobiological framework for risk and resilience
articles_hidden.authors: Isabelle Sjovall; Cleo Valentine; Lara Gregorians; Uemee Jung; Anjan Chatterjee; Esther Sternberg; Agustin Ibanez; Harris Eyre; John Kounios; Nicklas Berild Lundblad
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health is shaped by multiple factors, including the built environment. As urbanisation increases, urban living has been associated with higher rates of depression, anxiety and psychosis, although the evidence remains predominantly associative. Here, we synthesise epidemiological, neuroimaging and environmental research into a six-domain framework for understanding how built-environment qualities may relate to mental health risk and resilience. The domains comprise Safety and Accessibility, Cognitive Load and Environmental Complexity, Multisensory Integration, Emotional Valence, Social Connection, and Naturalness and Biophilia. We link these domains to neural, physiological, cognitive, emotional and social pathways, and outline methods for testing them across environmental, experiential and neurobiological levels. The framework provides a structure for developing more precise and testable hypotheses about how specific characteristics of the built environment may influence mental health and resilience.

articles_hidden.title: Imagining Oneself or the Object? Task-Dependent Effects in Mental Paper Folding and Body Rotation
articles_hidden.authors: Stephan Frederic Dahm; Carla Czilczer; Marcos Moreno-Verdú; Pierre Sachse
articles_hidden.abstract: While theoretical accounts of action imagery emphasize the role of the actor performing the movement, it remains unclear whether self-related kinesthetic imagery (self-imagery) compared to object-related visual imagery (object-imagery) supports mental transformations similarly for body-related and non-body stimuli. To clarify this relationship, 142 participants completed the mental paper folding task and the mental body rotation task under two imagery instructions: based on self-imagery or object-imagery. Instructions successfully shifted subjective imagery experiences, with self-imagery emphasizing bodily sensations and object-imagery emphasizing visualization. Performance analyses revealed robust task-specific effects: mental paper folding performance decreased with the number of folds and direction changes, and mental body rotation performance decreased for larger (than smaller) rotations, for front-view (than back-view) stimuli and for foot (than hand) stimuli. Crucially, errors did not significantly differ between imagery instructions. For response times, however, the relative advantage of the instructions was task-specific. Response times were shorter under self-imagery in mental body rotations but shorter under object-imagery in mental paper folding. Yet, in mental paper folding, this effect varied with instruction order, which might reflect a carryover effect of self-referential processing from self-imagery to object-imagery. Cross-task response times resulted in medium correlations when imagery instructions matched, whereas error rate correlations showed no consistent pattern. Overall, the findings indicate that the advantage of self-imagery versus object-imagery depends on task demands. They are consistent with flexible recruitment of imagery processes, while leaving open whether this reflects different configurations of a shared system or partly distinct motor and visuospatial strategies.

articles_hidden.title: From exposure to experience: Viewing nature activates parahippocampal cortex while subjective reports of naturalness are associated with reduced lateral occipital activity
articles_hidden.authors: Isabelle Sjovall; Lara Gregorians; Cleo Valentine; Uemee Jung; Pablo Fernandez Velasco; Eva Zita Patai; Fiona Zisch; Hugo Spiers
articles_hidden.abstract: The benefits of incorporating elements of nature into architectural settings to improve wellbeing and cognition has been explored in numerous studies. However, the brain dynamics associated with exposure to natural elements in architecture and the subjective experience of nature in such settings remains unclear. Here we examined fMRI data recorded while participants watched first-person-view movies of architectural spaces that varied in the extent to which they included natural elements (green space or water). These natural elements were decorrelated across movies from the other aspects of the movies, such as subject rated valence and layout complexity. This design also permitted dissociation of the visual presence of natural elements (exposure) from the subjective sense of connectedness to nature they elicit (experience), dimensions that are frequently conflated in the extant literature. Movies were rated for a range of qualities from the NeuroDesign/NeuroArchitecture Index (NDIX), which revealed that perceived connectedness to nature was partly dissociable from the presence of green space, water, luminance, layout complexity and valence of the spaces. Videos of spaces with nature were associated with increased activity in areas associated with scene processing and navigational affordances (parahippocampus, and occipital regions). Connectedness to nature was associated with a reduction in activation in bilateral lateral occipital regions. These results provide new insights into how natural features and the sense of naturalness in architectural spaces may affect brain regions that are linked to visual processing and affordances.

articles_hidden.title: Multi-study exploration across controlled indoor spaces: Initial evaluation of the feasibility and sensitivity of the NeuroDesign/NeuroArchitecture Index (NDIX)
articles_hidden.authors: Isabelle Sjovall; Uemee Jung; Cleo Valentine; Emre Yavuz; James Moultrie; Lucia Bussell; Lola Artiles San Juan; Jiang Zhu; George Joseph; John Draper
articles_hidden.abstract: People spend much of their lives in built environments, yet methods for evaluating how these environments are experienced remain limited. This research reports the first multi-study application of the NeuroDesign/NeuroArchitecture Index (NDIX), a multidimensional measure of environmental experience, and examines whether it is sensitive to meaningful differences between standard and environmentally enriched indoor spaces. Study 1 used a randomised repeated-measures crossover design in which 42 participants evaluated a standard quiet room and an enriched redesign of the same space. Study 2 (N = 40) evaluated standard and enriched innovation environments using complementary repeated-measures (n = 19) and independent-groups (n = 20 per group) comparisons. In both settings the instrument was administered in full in a single short session. In Study 1, NDIX Overall was higher in the enriched environment than in the standard environment (dz = 1.83), with higher scores across all six domains after false discovery rate correction and an equivalent effect in both presentation orders. Internal consistency was good for NDIX Overall (α = .87 and .89) but variable across domains (α = .40 to .77). Free-text descriptions of the most salient change centred on green plants, artwork and layout. Study 2 reproduced the pattern, with NDIX Overall higher in the enriched environment both within participants (dz = 2.50) and between independent groups (d = 1.90). The findings indicate that the NDIX is practical to administer and sensitive to meaningful environmental variation, while further psychometric evaluation is required across populations, environmental contexts, and more subtly differing settings.

articles_hidden.title: Meaningfulness shapes strategic memory use
articles_hidden.authors: Luzi Xu; Surya Gayet; Andre Sahakian; Chris Paffen; Stefan van der Stigchel
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent studies show that working memory for meaningful real-world objects can far exceed traditional capacity limits (~4 items) under experimental conditions where items are briefly presented. In everyday life, however, information often remains accessible, and observers freely choose how much to remember now and how much to inspect later. Under such unconstrained conditions, people typically memorize only 1–2 items at a time, far below maximum capacity. Here, we asked how meaningfulness influences strategic memory use during unconstrained memory-guided behavior. Using a copying task that allows for reinspections of the display, we compared meaningful real‑world objects with meaningless (novel‑but‑realistic) objects matched on low‑level visual features. Across two experiments, meaningfulness increased memory use, boosting it from ~2.5 items (meaningless objects) to ~3.8 items (meaningful objects) per sampling. Thus, the advantage of real‑world objects extends beyond capacity: it changes how people balance memory use against re-sampling of information in natural behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Building the future: Schemas contribute to episodic simulation
articles_hidden.authors: Sabrina Laurenne Valenzano; Isaac Kinley; Reece Pierre Roberts; Daniel L Schacter; Donna Rose Addis
articles_hidden.abstract: Future imagination is argued to rely on schematic knowledge and executive functions, yet direct evidence is lacking. Participants (N=50) completed executive measures and imagined future events involving schema-congruent or -incongruent objects and locations. Events were rated for detail and plausibility and scored for episodic content. We also collected descriptions of the locations in a separate sample (N=20) that served as proxies for culturally-shared schemas in a narrative representational similarity analysis (RSA): schema and event texts were converted into high-dimensional vectors using document embeddings, and cosine similarity was computed between vectors. RSA showed evidence of schema use: event narratives were most similar in meaning to schema descriptions of the same locations, particularly at the start of trials. Executive capacities were unrelated to schema use, although relational reasoning ability was associated with higher subjective detail on congruent trials. This study provides initial direct evidence of schema use in service of future imagining.

articles_hidden.title: Memorability as an Emergent Property: How Representational Structure Creates Apparent Intrinsic Effects
articles_hidden.authors: Dyllan Simpson; John Wixted; Timothy F. Brady
articles_hidden.abstract: Some pictures, videos, faces, voices, and words are reliably remembered better than others, a phenomenon known as memorability. This has been widely interpreted as reflecting a stable, intrinsic property of the stimuli themselves. Here we argue that this consistency is better explained by the relational structure of the stimulus sets used to measure memorability, rather than as an intrinsic property of the items. Using simulations with a global matching model of recognition memory, we show that apparent intrinsic memorability emerges naturally from distinctiveness — how dissimilar an item is from others in a given set of encoded images — without any stimulus-intrinsic mechanism. In behavioral experiments, we demonstrate that manipulating the similarity structure of image sets can invert memorability rankings, making previously memorable images forgettable and vice versa. We also show that features previously identified as intrinsically memorable (such as “body-part related”) are the most representationally distinctive features in standard databases, explaining their memorability. To address these large variations in distinctiveness we created a new image set that reduced variability in representational distinctiveness, and found it significantly diminishes all feature-memorability relationships. These findings suggest that memorability is not a fixed attribute of items themselves, but an emergent property of which items are distinctive within the context, with implications for how we attribute stable psychological properties to stimuli more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: Functional Structural Detachment: How Useful Perceptual Structure Carries Value Across Contexts
articles_hidden.authors: Jacek Rogala; Marek Kuś; Beata Bajno; Shabnam Kadir
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract forms can move us. A securely fixed sculpture can still look ready to fall and make us uneasy. Why does this visual pattern affect us when nothing can fall? We propose that what perceivers evaluate is often not an object as such but structure in sensory signals that carries information about the state and properties of objects and events. Deformation can indicate stiffness, the relation between mass and support can indicate stability, and visual expansion can signal approach. When such information matters for what a perceiver does or for what happens to them, the structure that carries it acquires evaluative weight. This structure is often available before the object is identified, and under poorer conditions: in the periphery, at a distance, in poor light, and for objects never seen before. Responding to it lets perceivers prepare to act early, at the price of responding wherever the structure appears, including in objects they cannot identify.
Some evaluative influence can remain when the information no longer serves its original use, which we call functional detachment (FD), and it can appear in new objects or events that preserve the same informative structure, which we call structural transfer. Together, they define functional structural detachment (FSD). The influence persists in part because a structure with little use in one context remains important in others.
FSD predicts that evaluative influence transfers further when the structure has a broad functional history, having been useful across many different situations, even when perceivers detect it equally well. We describe experiments that separate this account from salience, processing fluency, simple association, and the valuation of current consequences.
Art provides a limiting case: abstract forms can retain structures that were informative about objects and events elsewhere, and these structures can continue to affect us even when their original source and practical role have become remote.

articles_hidden.title: Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA): Nodal Variance Decomposition and Coefficient Gamma for Psychometric Networks
articles_hidden.authors: César Huerta-Huacchahuilca; Jano Ramos-Diaz
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychometric network analysis faces a foundational methodological divide: while rejecting the latent common-cause assumption, applied studies evaluate composite score reliability using classical common-cause coefficients (α, ω) or substitute metric precision with bootstrap partition frequencies (bootEGA), incurring indirect reliability induction under REGEMA guidelines and violating AERA/APA/NCME testing standards. We introduce Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA), an analytical framework grounded in support-constrained maximum likelihood refitting (K̂_refit) and the Neumann–Markov resolvent operator (Q = [I − Ω]⁻¹). rEGA establishes the Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad, partitioning standardized item variance into Within-Community Communality (hᵢ²), Inter-Community Bridging Variance (βᵢ²), and Markov Nodal Uniqueness (ψᵢ²), such that hᵢ² + βᵢ² + ψᵢ² ≡ 1.000. From this decomposition, rEGA defines a purity-weighted adjacency matrix (A^rEGA), Within-Community (Γ_c) and Total Network (Γ_t) reliability coefficients, and the Graph Standard Error of Measurement (SEM^raw). Across a Monte Carlo simulation of 97,200 datasets (972 conditions), rEGA-Leiden outperformed Walktrap, Louvain, and Parallel Analysis in dimensionality recovery (87.65% vs. 64.81%–71.32%), eliminated ℓ₁-shrinkage bias (RMSE_ψ = .035), classified core, bridge, and noise nodes with 86.8%–99.4% accuracy, and yielded unbiased reliability estimates (Bias_Γ = −.007) immune to lexical doublet inflation. Multi-sample validation on the AAQ-II (N = 3,200) and DASS-21 (N = 2,751) demonstrated that the Nodal Triad Leakage Criterion (β̄² > h̄²) rules out spurious over-fragmentation while distinguishing noisy items (A1) from transdiagnostic bridges (D2, S3, S6) with high cross-sample invariance (r > .93). Separating structural validity from score error, rEGA prevents ad hoc scale pruning and reconciles network psychometrics with international measurement standards.

articles_hidden.title: MDMA-Assisted Therapy for Social Anxiety Disorder: A Qualitative Analysis of Patient Experiences of Change
articles_hidden.authors: Christina Chwyl; Malena Donas; Angelica Spata; Gabriella Gatto; Akeesha Simmons; Kim Hoffman; M. Kati Lear; Brian Pilecki; Jenna LeJeune; Jason B Luoma
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: This study represents the first qualitative analysis to explore experiences of 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA)-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) for people with social anxiety disorder. 

Method: Following two MDMA (midomafetamine) sessions, participants (N = 20) completed semi-structured interviews of their treatment experiences. Team members derived themes pertaining to what aspects of treatment participants felt contributed to therapeutic benefit through reflexive thematic analysis.  

Results: Five themes were identified: 1) Healing Catalysed by Gently Facing Difficult Experiences (sub-themes: Moving from Criticism to Curiosity and Compassion; Enhanced Capacity to Access and Process Emotions); 2) Meaning Making through Broadened Perspectives of Self and Others (sub-themes: Clarity on the Origins of Distress; Deeper Understanding of Authentic Self; Interconnectedness and Oneness); 3) From Intellectual to Felt Knowing through Embodied States (sub-themes: Emotional Experiencing and Release; Feeling Safe and at Ease with Oneself); 4) Learning New Relational Patterns through Vulnerable Self-Expression; and 5) MDMA Experiences as Anchor for Ongoing Self-Discovery. 

Conclusion: Overall, participants felt that MDMA in the context of a safe therapeutic container facilitated them facing, deeply feeling and embodying emotions, which catalysed new insights and healing. By feeling more connected and at ease with themselves and with others, participants gained the motivation to show up authentically in their relationships.

articles_hidden.title: Owning the Gap: How Observers Judge the Distance Between What People Say They Want and What They Do
articles_hidden.authors: Shiyun Zhang Isabelle
articles_hidden.abstract: Observers evaluate more than what people achieve. They also evaluate how people stand toward the distance between an aspiration and their conduct. This paper proposes gap ownership as a construct for that stance. It follows Weber's ideal-type method as extended by Etzrodt. Three types are derived from two questions: whether the aspiration is kept, and whether the actor accepts authorship of the gap. In the owned gap, the actor answers for the distance. In the disowned gap, the actor keeps the aspiration, does not live it, and places its failure outside the self. In the dissolved gap, each aspiration is replaced before it is acted on. The last two correspond to the alienation and anomie poles in Etzrodt's reading of Weber. For a fixed gap, observers' respect, irritation, contempt, and discounting are predicted to depend on the stance, whatever the desirability of the aspiration. The claim has a domain. For obligations to others, a good excuse softens the listener. For self-regarding aspirations the paper predicts the reverse: answering for the gap earns more respect than explaining it away. Seven propositions carry refutation conditions, and rival predictions separate ownership from behavioral integrity, false signaling, listener burden, and the controllability of excuses.

articles_hidden.title: What You Notice Moves You More: Self-Reported Arousal Follows Noticed Changes in Paced Breathing
articles_hidden.authors: Norman A. S. Farb; Kyle Logie; Rose Amir Pour
articles_hidden.abstract: Does bodily change shape self-reported arousal only when it is noticed? In the Breath Change Awareness Task, participants breathe with a visual pacer or follow it by vision alone, report whether its pace changed, and rate arousal. After four development studies (Prolific adults and undergraduates, N = 579), we report a preregistered laboratory study (N = 206) with verified breathing. Arousal followed noticed changes more steeply than missed ones, with or without breathing, and in most studies noticed effects scaled with a change's size beyond the reported direction. In Study 5, missed changes moved arousal up to a third as much although breathing tracked the pacer closely, and a noticed breathed change moved arousal 1.8 [1.3, 2.7] times as much as one followed by vision alone, though not detectably in the online Study 4. Ratings partly followed the preceding detection report. Self-reported arousal mainly follows noticing; breathing adds to it.

articles_hidden.title: No evidence that overnight sleep improves associative inference
articles_hidden.authors: Johannes Wibroe; Shane Lindsay
articles_hidden.abstract: Sleep can help preserve learned associations, but evidence that it also helps people draw new inferences from them is mixed. We tested both outcomes in the same task, comparing performance after a 12-hour overnight interval with performance after a daytime interval of the same length. In an online experiment, participants learned overlapping object pairs (A–B and B–C) and were tested on them immediately and again after the delay. Only at the delayed test were they asked to infer the relationship between objects linked through the shared item (A–C). We analysed accuracy and response times using Bayesian multilevel models. Memory for the learned pairs declined in both groups, and inference accuracy remained close to chance. Inferences were more likely to be correct when participants also recognised both of the pairs needed to make them. Overall, the results gave no clear evidence of an overnight benefit for memory or inference and were consistent with participants retrieving and combining the learned pairs at test.

articles_hidden.title: Appetitive Food Rewards and Cognitive Flexibility: Reward Transitions, Voluntary Task Switching, and Individual Differences
articles_hidden.authors: Beatrice Lomeo; Joseph M Orr
articles_hidden.abstract: Motivation shapes how people allocate cognitive control, including whether they persist with a current task or flexibly switch to another. Although reward transitions have been shown to influence this balance, prior work has largely relied on monetary incentives. We tested whether changes in appetitive food reward motivate voluntary task switching, and whether this effect varies with subjective reward valuation and eating-related traits. A total of 112 undergraduate participants completed a voluntary task-switching task in which cues signaled low (1 point) or high (10 points) rewards exchangeable for candy. Access to the candy rewards was manipulated between subjects, with a free access group and a restricted group that could see, but not access, the received candy rewards. Trial-level choices were analyzed with generalized linear mixed models. Participants switched tasks more often when reward value changed between trials than when it remained consistently low or high. This reward-transition effect was larger among participants reporting greater candy liking and wanting. It was also stronger among those more susceptible to external food cues and weaker among those reporting greater routine restraint. Candy-access condition and progress toward the next candy did not improve model fit in the primary choice model. These findings identify reward dynamics as a motivational influence on cognitive flexibility and extend reward-transition accounts of control allocation to primary food incentives. Individual differences in incentive valuation and eating-related tendencies further shape how reward cues guide flexible behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Environmental Preference and Context-Supported Episodic Recall
articles_hidden.authors: Dylan Chau Huynh; Aja Khalid Hussein; Lars Brorson Fich; Yannick Joye; Zakaria Djebbara
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental preferences vary between individuals, yet little is known about how these preferences relate to memory for information encountered in different environments. We investigated this relationship in 60 participants using four virtual environments varying in environmental type (urban vs. natural) and spatial regularity (rhythmic vs. irregular). Participants completed immediate and delayed recall tasks, including two tasks assessing context-supported memory, and reported their general environmental preferences and preferences for the environments they experienced. General preferences for nature and spatial structure were not associated with memory performance. However, context-supported recall was higher for objects encountered in environments that participants subsequently identified as preferred. These findings highlight the relevance of individual evaluations of specific environments for understanding memory in everyday settings, suggesting that the cognitive implications of environmental design may depend not only on environmental characteristics but also on how individuals experience and evaluate them

articles_hidden.title: Can Human Verification Restore Felt Responsibility for AI-Assisted Knowledge Work?
articles_hidden.authors: Stefan Rose; Markus Weinmann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Generative AI (genAI) co-produces the work of hundreds of millions of people. Human
oversight, the default safeguard in AI governance, assumes that people still feel responsible
for the outputs they approve. Yet genAI assistance can lower psychological ownership of
such outputs, and whether the resulting loss of felt responsibility can be repaired remains
unclear. Drawing on the triangle model of responsibility and psychological ownership theory,
we propose that psychological ownership is how people experience the causal link between
themselves and an outcome, that genAI assistance weakens this link, and that a mandatory
verification step after generation can rebuild it. We derive five hypotheses on the erosion and
restoration of psychological ownership and felt responsibility and on revision after criticism,
and we outline a 3 × 2 experiment to test them.

articles_hidden.title: Indikationskatalog Musiktherapie in der neurologischen Rehabilitation
articles_hidden.authors: Monika Baumann; Stefan Mainka; Anna Badorrek; Silja Molle
articles_hidden.abstract: Der Indikationskatalog Musiktherapie in der neurologischen Rehabilitation gibt einen systematischen Überblick über die musiktherapeutische Praxis in diesem Bereich. Er verbindet wissenschaftliche Grundlagen und klinische Expertise, berücksichtigt den multidisziplinären Kontext und das spezifische Setting in der Neurorehabilitation und geht im Detail auf die Symptomatiken der Patient:innen ein. Der Katalog listet 5 Indikationsbereiche: Bewusstsein, Sensomotorik, Kommunikation, Kognition und Psyche. Für jeden Bereich werden in Tabellenform einzelnen Symptomen die jeweiligen Therapieziele und Interventionen zugeordnet. Das Spektrum der musiktherapeutischen Interventionen reicht von basalem Kontaktaufbau bei Menschen mit Bewusstseinsstörungen über funktionales Training bei motorischen, sprachlichen und kognitiven Beeinträchtigungen bis zur Behandlung psychischer Symptome. Dabei werden sowohl in anderen Fachbereichen übliche Methoden der aktiven und rezeptiven Musiktherapie aufgeführt als auch spezifische Methoden für die Arbeit mit neurologischen Patient:innen (einschließlich der neurologischen Musiktherapie®). So dient der Katalog gleichermaßen als Handlungsgrundlage für die musiktherapeutische Praxis als auch der Information benachbarter Disziplinen und der Kostenträger.

articles_hidden.title: Fast Eyes, Sharp Eyes, or Good Eyes? What Links Visual Perception to Higher-Order Cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Shanglin Yang; Rean Du; Jeffrey N. Rouder
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do simple perceptual tasks predict higher-order cognition, such as working memory and fluid intelligence? We contrast three hypotheses. Fast eyes: individuals who extract visual information quickly do well on both perceptual and cognitive tasks. Sharp eyes: individuals who resolve targets clearly in visual noise do well on both. Good eyes: a general visual ability, specific to neither speed nor noise, underlies both. To distinguish them, we crossed three stimulus types (Pi, letter, Gabor) with two masking types. In temporal masking, a mask follows the target and limits processing time; in spatial masking, the same mask accompanies the target and limits visibility through noise. Each task’s temporal and spatial versions thus shared the same stimulus and mask, differing only in how the mask was presented. 79 participants completed these perceptual tasks and four cognitive tasks. A hierarchical psychometric structural equation model decomposed individual differences into general visual, masking, and stimulus factors and related each to cognitive performance. The results show that masking type accounted for relatively little variance and was unrelated to cognitive performance. Stimulus type accounted for more variance but was also unrelated to cognitive performance. Only the general visual factor, shared across all perceptual tasks, was strongly related to cognitive performance (*r* = .64), supporting the good-eyes hypothesis.

articles_hidden.title: An MDS-REM Model for Predicting Individual-Item Perceptual Old-New Recognition
articles_hidden.authors: Robert Nosofsky; Adam F Osth
articles_hidden.abstract: The Retrieving Effectively for Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin & Stevyers, 1997) is an extremely influential model of old-new recognition memory based on Bayesian reasoning principles that provides a comprehensive account of diverse memory phenomena.  However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that it does not provide accounts of recognition memory at the level of individual items based on their precise positions in multidimensional similarity space and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.  Instead, it assumes a geometric probability distribution for generating hypothetical features and relies on computer simulation to generate predictions of patterns of results for large classes of items and experimental manipulations.  Here we move in the direction of filling that gap by proposing a REM-like model in which individual items are represented in one-to-one correspondence as points in multidimensional similarity (MDS) spaces and in which information regarding distinctive features possessed by individual objects is also provided.  Rather than using the geometric-probability distribution envisioned by Shiffrin and Steyvers, this “MDS-REM” model uses continuous probability density functions defined over the continuous-dimension MDS spaces.  The model is tested using data sets from three previously reported perceptual old-new recognition studies and provides reasonably accurate predictions of performance at the level of individual items or categories, including accounts of how both false-alarm and hit rates are influenced by detailed similarity relations among items and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating Safety in Reproductive Health Self-Care Interventions in Ghana: A Qualitative Study
articles_hidden.authors: Kwasi Adu Manu; Sarah E. Stutterheim; Charles Adjei; Francine Schneider
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction
Reproductive health self-care interventions are growing rapidly in Ghana, but there is limited evidence on the quality-of-care provisions that ensure safety for end-users and health professionals. This study explored how quality of care and safety are experienced and maintained within reproductive health self-care interventions in Ghana, using a self-care-specific conceptual framework.

Materials and Methods
Using an exploratory qualitative approach, underpinned by the Quality-of-Care Framework for Self-Care, we interviewed 29 end-users and 19 professionals, comprising health providers, program managers, digital referral agents, and community facilitators across Accra, Tamale, Cape Coast, and Sunyani. The study spanned six sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) domains: family planning, abortion, HIV/STI, maternal and child health, general SRHR, and cervical cancer. Data was analysed using thematic analysis techniques in Dedoose, grounded in both deductive and inductive principles.

Results
Key outcomes include the following: Technical Competency – Despite barriers, end-users felt sufficiently empowered to access self-care services. although professionals required continuous capacity strengthening to keep pace with the evolving ecosystem; Client Safety – End-users preferred access to medical eligibility information, but professionals were while professionals expressed concerns about potential misuse; Information Exchange – Information on family planning self-care services was more openly available than across other SRHR domains; Interpersonal Connection and Choice – End-users reported more positive experiences with remote services than facility-based care, although professionals faced operational constraints that affected consistent delivery of quality care; Continuity of Care – Follow-up care was better integrated across health facilities than alternate service delivery points, with periodic stockouts disrupting continuity efforts.

Conclusion
In exploring how quality of care and safety are experienced and maintained within reproductive health self-care interventions in Ghana, this study found that end-users and professionals have adopted interim measures to maintain some level of safety amid policy and institutional inadequacies. However, the sustainability of these measures is uncertain, posing a serious risk to public health if not prioritised in the short term.

articles_hidden.title: Personality Prediction from Moments to Lifetimes
articles_hidden.authors: Emorie D Beck; Adam Taylor Nissen; Eileen Kranz Graham; Dan Mroczek
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality is robustly linked to long-term outcomes, yet predicting momentary behavior (i.e., who does what, when, and where) remains challenging. We argue that personality and its outcomes can be understood at multiple levels within an emergent hierarchy, and that prediction requires identifying what level(s) is most informative for a given target. Broad traits reliably predict distal outcomes such as cognitive aging and mortality but reveal little about underlying processes. Within-person patterns capture shorter-term regularities, though heterogeneity is often overlooked. Momentary processes unfold as complex, multivariate systems that support personalized prediction but challenge generalization. We therefore propose a bottom-up integrative framework that derives comparable features from person-specific dynamics and tests whether they predict outcomes at other levels. Emerging evidence suggests that such features can bridge levels and support more integrative, explainable prediction.

articles_hidden.title: Thought for food: Individual differences in how food decisions are made
articles_hidden.authors: Caitlin Lloyd; Zarrar Shehzad; Janet Schebendach; Akram Bakkour; Alice M Xue; Naomi Assaf; Rayman Jiliani; B. Timothy Walsh; Daphna Shohamy; Joanna Steinglass
articles_hidden.abstract: Daily food decisions accumulate to impact physical health, but making choices consistent with longer-term health goals can prove challenging. Prior research has focused predominantly on dampening preferences for highly palatable foods, or exerting self-control, as the mechanism for healthier food choices. Consequently, the range of cognitive strategies for healthy eating, and how they vary with demographic characteristics, remains unclear. Here, a large US sample (N = 1,052) completed an online food rating and choice task, and demographic and eating behavior questionnaires. Participants rated foods across 17 dimensions, which were reduced to three underlying core food attributes by factor analysis: Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami (capturing food savoriness). All attributes influenced food choices. A multi-attribute drift diffusion model quantified distinct yet latent choice processes, including the deliberation required prior to making a choice. The influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami on choice varied across the study population. Women, individuals endorsing higher levels of eating restraint, and individuals with lower BMI selected subjectively healthier foods more frequently. Making subjectively healthier choices was not dependent only on engaging self-control. Rather, individuals making subjectively healthier choices perceived subjectively healthier foods as tastier. In addition, individuals endorsing high levels of eating restraint required less deliberation when making choices, suggesting more automatic decision-making. These findings suggest multiple routes to making healthier food choices and question the narrative that food tastiness must be sacrificed to support physical health.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of active learning and talker variability on preschoolers' novel word learning
articles_hidden.authors: Federica Bulgarelli; Marina Rabideau
articles_hidden.abstract: Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people. This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning. For example, 14-month-olds benefit from talker variability when learning minimal pairs, but struggle when learning distinct-sounding words. Talker variability is found to be particularly beneficial for learning to produce novel words. All of these previous studies have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability. Here, we used an active learning paradigm wherein preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning. Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them. We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, and talker variability choices interact with active learning to predict production, but not comprehension. Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children can make choices are benefit their own learning, informing theories of both talker variability and active learning.

articles_hidden.title: Theory of Mind and the Agreeableness-Antagonism Dimension: Differential Associations with Callousness, Aggression, and Manipulativeness
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle M. Berry; Scott D. Blain; Aisha Linnea Udochi; Muchen Xi; Colin G. DeYoung; Timothy Allen
articles_hidden.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) refers to how we identify and understand the mental states of others. ToM abilities vary with dimensions of normal-range personality and can be seriously impaired in a number of mental disorders, particularly those related to the Antagonism domain. The current study used a multi-task design to examine how ToM relates to Agreeableness-Antagonism subfactors, replicating and extending previous work. Participants (N = 335) completed self-report measures of the Big Five, empathy, and personality pathology, as well as tasks spanning mental state attribution, affect recognition, and mentalizing. Exploratory structural equation modeling was used to assess the impact of Agreeableness-Antagonism subfactors on ToM. A three-factor structure was derived for Agreeableness-Antagonism, with factors corresponding to Compassion-Callousness, Pacifism-Aggression, and Honesty-Manipulativeness. While higher Aggression and lower Compassion predicted worse ToM ability, higher Manipulativeness predicted better ToM ability. Findings replicate and extend work suggesting differential relations of specific Agreeableness-Antagonism subfactors with social cognition. We discuss our results with a focus on the importance of dimensional psychopathology models and facet-level research.

articles_hidden.title: Learning What Matters: Goal certainty shapes working memory prioritization
articles_hidden.authors: Cathy Zhang; Ata Baris Karagoz; Wouter Kool
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive resources are limited, yet people face an abundance of information. Often, which information matters is not stated and can change over time, so people must learn it through experience. This creates a tradeoff: uncertainty requires broad maintenance of multiple information sources, whereas certainty allows resources to be allocated more selectively. Does this reorganization of resources reflect enhancement of relevant information, degradation of irrelevant information, or both? Working memory provides a window into this process because differences in attentional priority should be reflected in what is remembered. To address these questions, we developed the Continuously Assessed Rule Inference Task, in which participants (N = 104) judged whether multidimensional stimuli followed a hidden rule that changed without warning, requiring them to continually update their beliefs about which information was relevant. On intermittent probe trials, participants reproduced the color, shape, and motion direction of the preceding stimulus. A reinforcement-learning model estimated trial-by-trial rule certainty from participants’ choices. As certainty increased, rule judgments relied more on evidence from the rule-defining (active) dimension, and memory for inactive features declined. A mixture model showed that active features became more likely to be retained, and inactive features less likely, with little evidence that the precision of retained features changed. These findings suggest that learning what matters reorganizes working memory by changing which information is retained, rather than how precisely it is represented. This shift from broad to selective maintenance may reflect a tradeoff between flexibility under uncertainty and efficiency once relevant information has been identified.

articles_hidden.title: Traveling back and forth through time: oscillatory brain patterns distinguish directional cued recall
articles_hidden.authors: Jeffrey D Johnson
articles_hidden.abstract: It is well established that episodic memory involves forming associations among stimuli within an event and between the event and its spatial and temporal context and that those associations can subsequently guide the strategies and search processes that lead to successful retrieval. While countless studies have characterized the neurocognitive correlates of relational memory, how retrieval precisely relies on the associations formed between consecutive events, as well as their correspondence with a representation of past time, is less understood. The current study sought to test how transitions are made across memories according to time by directly contrasting, behaviorally and neurally, retrieval in the forward versus backward directions. A list-learning paradigm was employed with immediate cued recall tasks in which subjects had to use cue words to recall those that came next (forward) or previously (backward) in the list. Scalp EEG data acquired just before the recalled words had to be reported was then used, in combination with multivariate pattern-classification analysis (MVPA), to distinguish neural activity related to retrieval deliberation and search processes. The main results provide novel evidence that, even while equating behavioral performance across retrieval direction, high-frequency (gamma-band) oscillatory EEG activity distinguishes forward and backward retrieval. Implications of the findings are discussed in relation to other, widely-used experimental and neuropsychological tasks (e.g., serial and free recall), as well as to work on understanding the broader role of time (i.e., past versus future) in episodic memory.
